before:
name: drawn_paint
description: >
  Drawn strokes become paint: six boxes that draw pen strokes with pressure on the document's
  drawing, read them back with notation, and paint them with afield.graphics.paint.PaintCanvas.

  `strokes` draws three strokes (a wave pressed hardest in the middle, a sweep that lifts off, a
  loop that bears down at its end) and plots the pen pressure along each. `paint` paints every
  stroke in that region three ways: with the brush's swell following the pen, following the pen's
  pressure squared, and at one even pressure. `crossings` draws yellow and red bands crossed by a
  vertical stroke four ways: blue into the wet bands (they mix), blue over the same bands dried,
  a clean hog brush smearing them, and a clean badger blender softening them. `drying` crosses one
  band after 0, 2, 10, 33 and 100 simulated hours. `meadow` paints a meadow at evening from 560
  strokes on a red-ground oil canvas with tube paints and a varnish glaze. `pencil` draws the
  strokes from `strokes` in a 6B pencil. Every box reads strokes from a region of the drawing, so
  strokes you draw there yourself (Alt+D, then P; a tablet pen records pressure) are painted too.
  The paint library is optional — `./gradlew buildPaintNative` builds it — and without it the
  painting boxes say so and stop.

  Companion to public/docs/chain_drawn_paint.md. Pure CPU; no Window, no Renderer, no audio device.
operations:
  - create:
      box: dp_strokes
      name: strokes
      frame: { x: 1750.0, y: 40.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          // Three pen strokes, drawn from code into the document's drawing, each with a pen pressure
          // (0..1) as a function of how far along the stroke the pen is. Running it again replaces them.
          notation {
              stroke(FLine().moveTo(80, 300).cubicTo(200, 60, 330, 420, 420, 140), name = "S",
                  pressure = { 0.15 + 0.85 * sin(PI * it) })
              stroke(FLine().moveTo(470, 110).cubicTo(560, 300, 700, 330, 820, 180), name = "sweep",
                  pressure = { 1.0 - 0.85 * it })
              stroke(FLine().moveTo(880, 330).cubicTo(1060, 300, 1020, 60, 900, 120).cubicTo(820, 160, 880, 260, 960, 250),
                  name = "loop", pressure = { 0.15 + 0.85 * it * it })
          }
          // Read back every stroke in this part of the drawing, with its pressure at 50 evenly spaced points.
          val strokes = notation.strokes.filter { it.bounds.intersects(Rect(40.0, 40.0, 1040.0, 400.0)) }
          showSignals(*strokes.map { (it.label ?: it.id) to it.pressuresAlong(50) }.toTypedArray(),
              x = (0 until 50).map { it / 49.0 }, title = "pen pressure along each stroke",
              xTitle = "fraction of the way along", yTitle = "pressure", channel = "pressure")
          markdown("table", "| stroke | points | lightest | heaviest |\n|---|---|---|---|\n" + strokes.joinToString("\n") {
              "| ${it.label ?: "drawn"} | ${it.points.size} | %.2f | %.2f |".format(it.pressures.minOrNull() ?: 0.0, it.pressures.maxOrNull() ?: 0.0)
          }, width = 380)
  - create:
      box: dp_paint
      name: paint
      frame: { x: 1750.0, y: 900.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.graphics.paint.*
          
          run {
          if (!PaintCanvas.isAvailable) {
              markdown(PaintLibrary.describe())
              return@run
          }
          // Every stroke in the region `strokes` drew in, painted three times, one row each: the brush
          // pressing as the pen did; the pen's pressure squared, so light strokes go lighter; one even pressure.
          val region = Rect(40.0, 40.0, 1040.0, 400.0)
          val strokes = notation.strokes.filter { it.bounds.intersects(region) }
          val colours = listOf(mapOf("ultramarine blue" to 2.0, "bone black" to 0.3), mapOf("vermilion" to 1.0), mapOf("viridian" to 1.0, "chrome yellow" to 0.6))
          val canvas = PaintCanvas(900, aspect = 0.9, view = Rect(40.0, 40.0, 1000.0, 1110.0))
          val brush = canvas.brush(BrushKind.Round, width = 70.0)
          fun lower(s: Mark, dy: Double) = FLine().also { f -> s.points.forEachIndexed { k, p -> if (k == 0) f.moveTo(p.x, p.y + dy) else f.lineTo(p.x, p.y + dy) } }
          strokes.forEachIndexed { i, s ->
              val pen = s.pressuresAlong(64)
              brush.load(colours[i % 3], wipe = 1.0)
              canvas.stroke(s.toFLine(), brush, pressure = 1.0..1.0, swell = pen)
              brush.load(colours[i % 3], wipe = 1.0)
              canvas.stroke(lower(s, 360.0), brush, pressure = 1.0..1.0, swell = pen.map { it * it })
              brush.load(colours[i % 3], wipe = 1.0)
              canvas.stroke(lower(s, 720.0), brush, pressure = 0.6..0.6)
          }
          display("main", canvas.png())
          }
  - create:
      box: dp_crossings
      name: crossings
      frame: { x: 1750.0, y: 2100.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.graphics.paint.*
          
          run {
          if (!PaintCanvas.isAvailable) {
              markdown(PaintLibrary.describe())
              return@run
          }
          // Four pairs of bands, yellow over red, each crossed by one vertical stroke.
          notation {
              for (k in 0 until 4) {
                  val x = 60.0 + k * 250
                  stroke(FLine().moveTo(x, 560).cubicTo(x + 70, 545, x + 140, 575, x + 210, 560), name = "yellow $k", pressure = { 0.8 })
                  stroke(FLine().moveTo(x, 760).cubicTo(x + 70, 745, x + 140, 775, x + 210, 760), name = "red $k", pressure = { 0.8 })
                  stroke(FLine().moveTo(x + 95, 480).cubicTo(x + 120, 600, x + 90, 720, x + 115, 860), name = "across $k",
                      pressure = { 0.5 + 0.5 * sin(PI * it) })
              }
          }
          val canvas = PaintCanvas(900, aspect = 2.4, view = Rect(40.0, 460.0, 1000.0, 416.0))
          fun paint(name: String, brush: PaintBrush) = notation.named(name)!!.let {
              canvas.stroke(it.toFLine(), brush, pressure = 1.0..1.0, swell = it.pressuresAlong(32), shake = 0.5)
          }
          val band = canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width = 70.0)
          for (k in 0 until 4) {
              paint("yellow $k", band.load(mapOf("cadmium yellow" to 1.0), wipe = 1.0))
              paint("red $k", band.load(mapOf("vermilion" to 1.0), wipe = 1.0))
          }
          // 1: blue straight across the wet bands, so the colours mix where they meet
          paint("across 0", canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width = 60.0).load(mapOf("ultramarine blue" to 1.0)))
          // 3: a clean, dry hog-hair brush dragged through them: no paint of its own, it smears theirs
          paint("across 2", canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width = 60.0))
          // 4: a clean badger blender, which only softens what is there
          paint("across 3", canvas.brush(BrushKind.Badger, width = 60.0))
          // 2: the same blue, after everything has dried
          canvas.dry()
          paint("across 1", canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width = 60.0).load(mapOf("ultramarine blue" to 1.0)))
          display("main", canvas.png())
          }
  - create:
      box: dp_drying
      name: drying
      frame: { x: 1750.0, y: 2700.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.graphics.paint.*
          
          run {
          if (!PaintCanvas.isAvailable) {
              markdown(PaintLibrary.describe())
              return@run
          }
          // One yellow band, crossed in blue after longer and longer waits.
          val hours = listOf(0.0, 2.0, 10.0, 33.0, 100.0)
          notation {
              stroke(FLine().moveTo(60, 1080).cubicTo(400, 1070, 700, 1090, 1020, 1080), name = "slow band", pressure = { 0.85 })
              hours.indices.forEach { i ->
                  val x = 150.0 + i * 190
                  stroke(FLine().moveTo(x, 960).lineTo(x + 20, 1200), name = "after $i", pressure = { 0.5 + 0.5 * sin(PI * it) })
              }
          }
          val canvas = PaintCanvas(900, aspect = 3.2, view = Rect(40.0, 940.0, 1000.0, 312.0))
          fun paint(name: String, brush: PaintBrush) = notation.named(name)!!.let {
              canvas.stroke(it.toFLine(), brush, pressure = 1.0..1.0, swell = it.pressuresAlong(32), shake = 0.4)
          }
          paint("slow band", canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width = 80.0).load(mapOf("cadmium yellow" to 1.0)))
          var waited = 0.0
          hours.forEachIndexed { i, h ->
              canvas.wait((h - waited) * 60); waited = h      // simulated minutes
              paint("after $i", canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width = 60.0).load(mapOf("ultramarine blue" to 1.0)))
          }
          display("main", canvas.png())
          markdown("times", "crossed after " + hours.joinToString(", ") { "${it.toInt()} h" } + " (left to right)", width = 500)
          }
  - create:
      box: dp_meadow
      name: meadow
      frame: { x: 1750.0, y: 3200.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.graphics.paint.*
          import kotlin.random.Random
          
          run {
          if (!PaintCanvas.isAvailable) {
              markdown(PaintLibrary.describe())
              return@run
          }
          // A meadow at evening, from 560 pen strokes on the drawing. The strokes are drawn by code here
          // (a seeded random hand) into the region below; draw your own there instead and paint those.
          val region = Rect(40.0, 1460.0, 1600.0, 1000.0)
          val X = region.x
          val Y = region.y
          val rnd = Random(7)
          fun r(a: Double, b: Double) = rnd.nextDouble(a, b)
          fun sweep(x: Double, y: Double, w: Double, dy: Double = 0.0) =
              FLine().moveTo(X + x, Y + y).cubicTo(X + x + w * 0.3, Y + y - 20, X + x + w * 0.7, Y + y + 20, X + x + w, Y + y + dy)
          notation {
              for (i in 0 until 18) stroke(sweep(r(-160.0, 0.0), 20.0 + i * 26 + r(-6.0, 6.0), 1760.0, r(-10.0, 10.0)),   // sky
                  name = "sky $i", pressure = { 0.5 + 0.5 * sin(PI * it) })
              for (c in 0 until 5) {                                                                                  // clouds
                  val cx = r(150.0, 1350.0); val cy = r(90.0, 300.0)
                  for (k in 0 until 7) stroke(sweep(cx + r(-120.0, 80.0), cy + r(-35.0, 25.0), r(80.0, 220.0), 4.0),
                      name = "cloud $c.$k", pressure = { 0.2 + 0.8 * sin(PI * it) })
              }
              for (i in 0 until 5) stroke(sweep(-80.0, 500.0 + i * 10, 1760.0, -40.0),                                 // far hills
                  name = "hill $i", pressure = { 0.4 + 0.6 * sin(PI * it) })
              for (i in 0 until 22) stroke(sweep(-80.0, 540.0 + i * 22, 1760.0),                                       // the field
                  name = "field $i", pressure = { 0.7 + 0.3 * sin(PI * it) })
              for (i in 0 until 420) {                                                                                // grass
                  val y = r(560.0, 1000.0); val d = (y - 540) / 460; val x = r(-20.0, 1620.0)
                  val h = r(40.0, 120.0) + 300 * d * d; val lean = r(-0.3, 0.5) * h
                  stroke(FLine().moveTo(X + x, Y + y).cubicTo(X + x + lean * 0.1, Y + y - h * 0.5, X + x + lean * 0.5, Y + y - h * 0.9, X + x + lean, Y + y - h),
                      name = "grass $i", pressure = { 1.0 - 0.95 * it })                                              // flicked up from the root
              }
              for (i in 0 until 60) {                                                                                 // poppies
                  val y = r(570.0, 990.0); val x = r(40.0, 1560.0); val s = 4.0 + 22 * (y - 540) / 460
                  stroke(FLine().moveTo(X + x - s, Y + y).cubicTo(X + x - s * 0.3, Y + y - s, X + x + s * 0.5, Y + y - s * 0.8, X + x + s, Y + y + s * 0.2),
                      name = "poppy $i", pressure = { 0.5 + 0.5 * sin(PI * it) })
              }
          }
          
          val canvas = PaintCanvas(1200, aspect = 1.6, ground = PaintGround.OilRedGround, view = region)
          val strokes = notation.strokes.filter { it.bounds.intersects(region) }
          fun named(p: String) = strokes.filter { it.label?.startsWith(p) == true }
          fun depth(s: Mark) = ((s.start!!.y - Y - 540) / 460).coerceIn(0.0, 1.0)   // 0 at the horizon, 1 at the front
          fun paint(s: Mark, b: PaintBrush, p: Double = 1.0, shake: Double = 1.0) =
              canvas.stroke(s.toFLine(), b, pressure = p..p, swell = s.pressuresAlong(32), shake = shake)
          
          val sky = canvas.brush(BrushKind.Filbert, width = 60.0)
          named("sky").forEachIndexed { i, s ->
              val t = i / 17.0   // cobalt at the top, warming to Naples yellow and a little rose at the horizon
              paint(s, sky.load(mapOf("lead white" to 3.0, "cobalt blue" to 2.0 * (1 - t) * (1 - t), "Naples yellow" to 2.5 * t * t, "rose madder" to 0.4 * t), wipe = 0.5))
          }
          val cloud = canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width = 34.0)
          named("cloud").forEach { paint(it, cloud.load(Tubes.mix(mapOf("lead white" to 4.0, "Naples yellow" to 0.4, "rose madder" to 0.1)), hiding = 0.5, wipe = 0.3), shake = 0.8) }
          val hill = canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width = 26.0)
          named("hill").forEachIndexed { i, s -> paint(s, hill.load(mapOf("lead white" to 3.0 - i * 0.4, "cobalt blue" to 1.0, "green earth" to 1.0 + i * 0.4), wipe = 0.6)) }
          val field = canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width = 50.0)
          named("field").forEachIndexed { i, s ->
              val t = i / 21.0
              paint(s, field.load(mapOf("green earth" to 2.0, "yellow ochre" to 2.0 * (1 - t), "raw umber" to 1.5 * t, "lead white" to 1.0 * (1 - t)), wipe = 0.5))
          }
          canvas.wait(40.0)   // let the field set a little before the grass goes into it
          val grass = canvas.brush(BrushKind.Round, width = 10.0)
          val greens = listOf(mapOf("viridian" to 1.0, "yellow ochre" to 1.5), mapOf("green earth" to 2.0, "chrome yellow" to 1.0),
              mapOf("viridian" to 1.0, "raw umber" to 1.0), mapOf("yellow ochre" to 2.0, "lead white" to 1.0),
              mapOf("Prussian blue" to 0.2, "chrome yellow" to 2.0), mapOf("Naples yellow" to 2.0, "green earth" to 1.0))
          named("grass").sortedBy { it.start!!.y }.forEachIndexed { i, s -> paint(s, grass.load(greens[i % greens.size], wipe = 0.5), 0.4 + 0.6 * depth(s), shake = 0.6) }
          val poppy = canvas.brush(BrushKind.Filbert, width = 24.0)
          named("poppy").sortedBy { it.start!!.y }.forEach { s -> paint(s, poppy.load(mapOf("vermilion" to 3.0, "cadmium red" to 1.0, "lead white" to 0.2), wipe = 0.9), 0.3 + 0.7 * depth(s)) }
          canvas.dry()
          canvas.glaze(rgb(0.6, 0.45, 0.2), coats = 0.12)   // a thin warm varnish over the whole thing
          display("main", canvas.png())
          }
  - create:
      box: dp_pencil
      name: pencil
      frame: { x: 1750.0, y: 4200.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.graphics.paint.*
          
          run {
          if (!PaintCanvas.isAvailable) {
              markdown(PaintLibrary.describe())
              return@run
          }
          // The strokes from `strokes` in a 6B pencil, on a 20 cm sheet, its pressure following the pen.
          val region = Rect(40.0, 40.0, 1040.0, 400.0)
          val canvas = PaintCanvas(900, aspect = 3.0, view = Rect(40.0, 40.0, 1040.0, 347.0), sizeMm = 200.0)
          val pencil = canvas.pencil("6B")
          for (s in notation.strokes.filter { it.bounds.intersects(region) })
              canvas.draw(s.toFLine(), pencil, pressure = s.pressuresAlong(32).ifEmpty { listOf(0.6) })
          display("main", canvas.png())
          }
  - execute:
      box: dp_strokes
      property: code
  - execute:
      box: dp_paint
      property: code
  - execute:
      box: dp_crossings
      property: code
  - execute:
      box: dp_drying
      property: code
  - execute:
      box: dp_meadow
      property: code
  - execute:
      box: dp_pencil
      property: code

                  stroke(FLine().moveTo(x, 960).lineTo(x + 20, 1200), name = "after $i", pressure = { 0.5 + 0.5 * sin(PI * it) })
              }
          }
          val canvas = PaintCanvas(900, aspect = 3.2, view = Rect(40.0, 940.0, 1000.0, 312.0))
          fun paint(name: String, brush: PaintBrush) = notation.named(name)!!.let {
              canvas.stroke(it.toFLine(), brush, pressure = 1.0..1.0, swell = it.pressuresAlong(32), shake = 0.4)
          }
          paint("slow band", canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width = 80.0).load(mapOf("cadmium yellow" to 1.0)))
          var waited = 0.0
          hours.forEachIndexed { i, h ->
              canvas.wait((h - waited) * 60); waited = h      // simulated minutes
              paint("after $i", canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width = 60.0).load(mapOf("ultramarine blue" to 1.0)))
          }
          display("main", canvas.png())
          markdown("times", "crossed after " + hours.joinToString(", ") { "${it.toInt()} h" } + " (left to right)", width = 500)
          }
  - create:
      box: dp_meadow
      name: meadow
      frame: { x: 1750.0, y: 3200.0, w: 190.0, h: 60.0 }
      properties:
        code: |
          import afield.graphics.paint.*
          import kotlin.random.Random
          
          run {
          if (!PaintCanvas.isAvailable) {
              markdown(PaintLibrary.describe())
              return@run
          }
          // A meadow at evening, from 560 pen strokes on the drawing. The strokes are drawn by code here
          // (a seeded random hand) into the region below; draw your own there instead and paint those.
          val region = Rect(40.0, 1460.0, 1600.0, 1000.0)
          val X = region.x
          val Y = region.y
          val rnd = Random(7)
          fun r(a: Double, b: Double) = rnd.nextDouble(a, b)
          fun sweep(x: Double, y: Double, w: Double, dy: Double = 0.0) =
              FLine().moveTo(X + x, Y + y).cubicTo(X + x + w * 0.3, Y + y - 20, X + x + w * 0.7, Y + y + 20, X + x + w, Y + y + dy)
          notation {
              for (i in 0 until 18) stroke(sweep(r(-160.0, 0.0), 20.0 + i * 26 + r(-6.0, 6.0), 1760.0, r(-10.0, 10.0)),   // sky
                  name = "sky $i", pressure = { 0.5 + 0.5 * sin(PI * it) })
              for (c in 0 until 5) {                                                                                  // clouds
                  val cx = r(150.0, 1350.0); val cy = r(90.0, 300.0)
                  for (k in 0 until 7) stroke(sweep(cx + r(-120.0, 80.0), cy + r(-35.0, 25.0), r(80.0, 220.0), 4.0),
                      name = "cloud $c.$k", pressure = { 0.2 + 0.8 * sin(PI * it) })
              }
              for (i in 0 until 5) stroke(sweep(-80.0, 500.0 + i * 10, 1760.0, -40.0),                                 // far hills
                  name = "hill $i", pressure = { 0.4 + 0.6 * sin(PI * it) })
              for (i in 0 until 22) stroke(sweep(-80.0, 540.0 + i * 22, 1760.0),                                       // the field
                  name = "field $i", pressure = { 0.7 + 0.3 * sin(PI * it) })
              for (i in 0 until 420) {                                                                                // grass
                  val y = r(560.0, 1000.0); val d = (y - 540) / 460; val x = r(-20.0, 1620.0)
                  val h = r(40.0, 120.0) + 300 * d * d; val lean = r(-0.3, 0.5) * h
                  stroke(FLine().moveTo(X + x, Y + y).cubicTo(X + x + lean * 0.1, Y + y - h * 0.5, X + x + lean * 0.5, Y + y - h * 0.9, X + x + lean, Y + y - h),
                      name = "grass $i", pressure = { 1.0 - 0.95 * it })                                              // flicked up from the root
              }
              for (i in 0 until 60) {                                                                                 // poppies
                  val y = r(570.0, 990.0); val x = r(40.0, 1560.0); val s = 4.0 + 22 * (y - 540) / 460
                  stroke(FLine().moveTo(X + x - s, Y + y).cubicTo(X + x - s * 0.3, Y + y - s, X + x + s * 0.5, Y + y - s * 0.8, X + x + s, Y + y + s * 0.2),
                      name = "poppy $i", pressure = { 0.5 + 0.5 * sin(PI * it) })
              }
          }
          
          val canvas = PaintCanvas(1200, aspect = 1.6, ground = PaintGround.OilRedGround, view = region)
          val strokes = notation.strokes.filter { it.bounds.intersects(region) }
          fun named(p: String) = strokes.filter { it.label?.startsWith(p) == true }
          fun depth(s: Mark) = ((s.start!!.y - Y - 540) / 460).coerceIn(0.0, 1.0)   // 0 at the horizon, 1 at the front
          fun paint(s: Mark, b: PaintBrush, p: Double = 1.0, shake: Double = 1.0) =
              canvas.stroke(s.toFLine(), b, pressure = p..p, swell = s.pressuresAlong(32), shake = shake)
          
          val sky = canvas.brush(BrushKind.Filbert, width = 60.0)
          named("sky").forEachIndexed { i, s ->
              val t = i / 17.0   // cobalt at the top, warming to Naples yellow and a little rose at the horizon
              paint(s, sky.load(mapOf("lead white" to 3.0, "cobalt blue" to 2.0 * (1 - t) * (1 - t), "Naples yellow" to 2.5 * t * t, "rose madder" to 0.4 * t), wipe = 0.5))
          }
          val cloud = canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width = 34.0)
          named("cloud").forEach { paint(it, cloud.load(Tubes.mix(mapOf("lead white" to 4.0, "Naples yellow" to 0.4, "rose madder" to 0.1)), hiding = 0.5, wipe = 0.3), shake = 0.8) }
          val hill = canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width = 26.0)
          named("hill").forEachIndexed { i, s -> paint(s, hill.load(mapOf("lead white" to 3.0 - i * 0.4, "cobalt blue" to 1.0, "green earth" to 1.0 + i * 0.4), wipe = 0.6)) }
          val field = canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width = 50.0)
          named("field").forEachIndexed { i, s ->
              val t = i / 21.0
              paint(s, field.load(mapOf("green earth" to 2.0, "yellow ochre" to 2.0 * (1 - t), "raw umber" to 1.5 * t, "lead white" to 1.0 * (1 - t)), wipe = 0.5))
          }
          canvas.wait(40.0)   // let the field set a little before the grass goes into it
          val grass = canvas.brush(BrushKind.Round, width = 10.0)
          val greens = listOf(mapOf("viridian" to 1.0, "yellow ochre" to 1.5), mapOf("green earth" to 2.0, "chrome yellow" to 1.0),
              mapOf("viridian" to 1.0, "raw umber" to 1.0), mapOf("yellow ochre" to 2.0, "lead white" to 1.0),
              mapOf("Prussian blue" to 0.2, "chrome yellow" to 2.0), mapOf("Naples yellow" to 2.0, "green earth" to 1.0))
          named("grass").sortedBy { it.start!!.y }.forEachIndexed { i, s -> paint(s, grass.load(greens[i % greens.size], wipe = 0.5), 0.4 + 0.6 * depth(s), shake = 0.6) }
          val poppy = canvas.brush(BrushKind.Filbert, width = 24.0)
          named("poppy").sortedBy { it.start!!.y }.forEach { s -> paint(s, poppy.load(mapOf("vermilion" to 3.0, "cadmium red" to 1.0, "lead white" to 0.2), wipe = 0.9), 0.3 + 0.7 * depth(s)) }
          canvas.dry()
          canvas.glaze(rgb(0.6, 0.45, 0.2), coats = 0.12)   // a thin warm varnish over the whole thing
          display("main", canvas.png())
          }
  - create:
      box: dp_pencil

          }

          val canvas = PaintCanvas(900, aspect = 3.0, view = Rect(40.0, 40.0, 1040.0, 347.0), sizeMm = 200.0)

          for (s in notation.strokes.filter { it.bounds.intersects(region) })

name: fline_exact_booleans
description: >
  Curve-preserving booleans and cubic offsets for FLine, the companion to the "Exact booleans and
  offsets" section of `public/docs/fline_examples.md`. Two boxes, each drawing the old path on
  the left and the exact one on the right, with a dot on every node so the segment count is
  visible: (1) the union and difference of a circle and a blob through java.awt.geom.Area and
  through `booleanExact`; (2) a star and an open S-curve offset by `byOffsetting` (sampled
  polyline) and by `byOffsettingExact` (cubics with round joins). Run each box; each draws into
  `lines`.
operations:
  - create:
      box: fline-exact-booleans
      name: 1 - Booleans, Area (left) and exact (right)
      frame:
        x: 60.0
        y: 60.0
        w: 460.0
        h: 100.0
      properties:
        code: |
          fun circle(cx: Double, cy: Double, r: Double) = fline {
              val k = 0.5522847 * r
              moveTo(cx + r, cy)
              cubicTo(cx + r, cy + k, cx + k, cy + r, cx, cy + r)
              cubicTo(cx - k, cy + r, cx - r, cy + k, cx - r, cy)
              cubicTo(cx - r, cy - k, cx - k, cy - r, cx, cy - r)
              cubicTo(cx + k, cy - r, cx + r, cy - k, cx + r, cy)
              close()
          }

          fun blob(x: Double, y: Double) = fline {
              moveTo(x, y)
              cubicTo(x + 40, y - 30, x + 90, y + 10, x + 100, y + 50)
              cubicTo(x + 110, y + 90, x + 60, y + 70, x + 50, y + 110)
              cubicTo(x + 40, y + 150, x - 20, y + 120, x - 10, y + 80)
              cubicTo(x, y + 50, x - 30, y + 30, x, y)
              close()
          }

          // a dot on every node: how many segments each answer used
          fun dots(f: FLine, c: Vec4) = f.nodes.mapNotNull { it.toOrNull }.map { p ->
              fline {
                  moveTo(p.x + 2.5, p.y)
                  cubicTo(p.x + 2.5, p.y + 1.4, p.x + 1.4, p.y + 2.5, p.x, p.y + 2.5)
                  cubicTo(p.x - 1.4, p.y + 2.5, p.x - 2.5, p.y + 1.4, p.x - 2.5, p.y)
                  cubicTo(p.x - 2.5, p.y - 1.4, p.x - 1.4, p.y - 2.5, p.x, p.y - 2.5)
                  cubicTo(p.x + 1.4, p.y - 2.5, p.x + 2.5, p.y - 1.4, p.x + 2.5, p.y)
                  filled = true
                  stroked = false
                  color = c
              }
          }

          val out = mutableListOf<FLine>()
          for ((row, op) in listOf(FLineBooleanOp.Union, FLineBooleanOp.Subtract).withIndex()) {
              val y = 40.0 + row * 190
              for (col in 0..1) {
                  val x = 40.0 + col * 260
                  val a = blob(x + 20, y)
                  val b = circle(x + 90, y + 60, 45.0)
                  val r = if (col == 1) a.booleanExact(b, op).line
                      else if (op == FLineBooleanOp.Union) a.byUnionWith(b) else a.byDifferenceWith(b)
                  r.filled = true
                  r.stroked = true
                  r.thickness = 1.5
                  r.color = if (col == 0) vec(1.0, 0.55, 0.35, 0.35) else vec(0.4, 0.9, 1.0, 0.35)
                  out.add(r)
                  out.addAll(dots(r, if (col == 0) vec(1.0, 0.4, 0.2, 1.0) else vec(0.3, 0.8, 1.0, 1.0)))
                  println("$op ${if (col == 0) "Area" else "exact"}: ${r.segmentCount2D()} segments")
              }
          }
          lines(out, w = 460.0, h = 380.0, fitToSize = true)
  - create:
      box: fline-exact-offsets
      name: 2 - Offsets, sampled (left) and exact (right)
      frame:
        x: 560.0
        y: 60.0
        w: 460.0
        h: 100.0
      properties:
        code: |
          fun star(cx: Double, cy: Double) = fline {
              for (i in 0 until 10) {
                  val r = if (i % 2 == 0) 70.0 else 32.0
                  val a = kotlin.math.PI * i / 5
                  if (i == 0) moveTo(cx + r * kotlin.math.cos(a), cy + r * kotlin.math.sin(a))
                  else lineTo(cx + r * kotlin.math.cos(a), cy + r * kotlin.math.sin(a))
              }
              close()
          }

          fun sCurve(x: Double, y: Double) = fline {
              moveTo(x, y)
              cubicTo(x + 40, y - 55, x + 70, y + 55, x + 110, y)
              cubicTo(x + 140, y - 35, x + 170, y + 30, x + 200, y + 5)
              lineTo(x + 215, y + 55)
          }

          fun dots(f: FLine, c: Vec4) = f.nodes.mapNotNull { it.toOrNull }.map { p ->
              fline {
                  moveTo(p.x + 2.0, p.y)
                  cubicTo(p.x + 2.0, p.y + 1.1, p.x + 1.1, p.y + 2.0, p.x, p.y + 2.0)
                  cubicTo(p.x - 1.1, p.y + 2.0, p.x - 2.0, p.y + 1.1, p.x - 2.0, p.y)
                  cubicTo(p.x - 2.0, p.y - 1.1, p.x - 1.1, p.y - 2.0, p.x, p.y - 2.0)
                  cubicTo(p.x + 1.1, p.y - 2.0, p.x + 2.0, p.y - 1.1, p.x + 2.0, p.y)
                  filled = true
                  stroked = false
                  color = c
              }
          }

          val out = mutableListOf<FLine>()
          for (col in 0..1) {
              val x = 30.0 + col * 280
              val shapes = listOf(star(x + 110, 100.0), sCurve(x, 270.0))
              for (s in shapes) {
                  s.thickness = 1.0
                  s.color = vec(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.6)
                  out.add(s)
                  for (d in listOf(12.0, -12.0)) {
                      val o = if (col == 0) s.byOffsetting(d.toFloat()) else s.byOffsettingExact(d.toFloat())
                      o.thickness = 1.5
                      o.color = if (col == 0) vec(1.0, 0.55, 0.35, 1.0) else vec(0.4, 0.9, 1.0, 1.0)
                      out.add(o)
                      out.addAll(dots(o, if (col == 0) vec(1.0, 0.4, 0.2, 1.0) else vec(0.3, 0.8, 1.0, 1.0)))
                      println("${if (col == 0) "byOffsetting" else "byOffsettingExact"} d=$d: ${o.segmentCount2D()} segments")
                  }
              }
          }
          lines(out, w = 560.0, h = 360.0, fitToSize = true)
  - execute:
      box: fline-exact-booleans
      property: code
      type: fragment
  - execute:
      box: fline-exact-offsets
      property: code
      type: fragment

before:
# Differentiating Functions

Field computes exact derivatives of the code you write, by automatic differentiation. Reverse mode
over `Double` gives gradients, second-order forward mode gives curvature, and SGD, Adam and L-BFGS
minimize using either. An `Fn` built from stdlib parts can be differentiated too, with respect to
its own numeric parameters.

## One expression, three ways of differentiating it

`AD` is a `Double` that remembers how it was made. Arithmetic on it appends to a tape; a single
backward sweep reads off every derivative at once. `grad { }` returns a function, so you can hand it
straight to an optimizer.

`Dual2` works the other way around, carrying a value with its first and second derivatives
`(v, v', v'')` along a single direction. Use it when there is one input and many outputs; it is also
what makes `hessian` exact. The second derivative comes with the forward pass, so all three curves
below come from one sweep.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/autodiff_examples/derivatives.png" wait="2.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="600" padding="16"}
:::static
// The same expression, differentiated by a tape sweep, by a Taylor number, and by a central
// difference. If any two of them disagree, one of them is wrong.
val xs = (0..300).map { it / 300.0 * 2.0 - 1.0 }
val taylor = xs.map { x -> taylor2(x) { u -> exp(-u * u) * sin(6.0 * u) } }
val reverse = xs.map { x -> derivative(x) { u -> exp(-u * u) * sin(6.0 * u) } }
val oracle = xs.map { x ->
    val plain = { u: Double -> kotlin.math.exp(-u * u) * kotlin.math.sin(6.0 * u) }
    (plain(x + 1e-6) - plain(x - 1e-6)) / 2e-6
}

// The exact Hessian of Rosenbrock: one Dual2 pass gives vT H v, and polarisation recovers the
// off-diagonals. Not a finite difference of a gradient.
val h = hessian(doubleArrayOf(-1.2, 1.0)) { p -> (1.0 - p[0]).sq() + 100.0 * (p[1] - p[0].sq()).sq() }
val g = grad { p: List<AD> -> (1.0 - p[0]).sq() + 100.0 * (p[1] - p[0].sq()).sq() }
:::fold draw the three orders and report the agreement
showSignals(
    "f" to taylor.map { it.value },
    "f' (reverse mode)" to reverse,
    "f'' (forward mode)" to taylor.map { it.second },
    x = xs,
    title = "exp(-x^2)*sin(6x), its slope and its curvature - one sweep, three orders",
    xTitle = "x"
)
val worstPair = xs.indices.maxOf { kotlin.math.abs(taylor[it].first - reverse[it]) }
val worstOracle = xs.indices.maxOf { kotlin.math.abs(reverse[it] - oracle[it]) }
val agreement =
    "grad Rosenbrock at (-1.2, 1.0) = " + g(doubleArrayOf(-1.2, 1.0)).toList() + "\n" +
    "exact Hessian there            = [[" + h[0][0] + ", " + h[0][1] + "], [" + h[1][0] + ", " + h[1][1] + "]]\n" +

## Differentiating an `Fn` graph

Every `Fn` the stdlib builds carries a graph of the operations that made it, and Field can
differentiate that graph. So when you fit an `Fn` to a target, the gradient of the error with
respect to its numeric parameters is exact.

The example runs the same `fitGradient` twice, once with finite-difference gradients and once with
exact ones. The optimizer, step size and target are the same.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/autodiff_examples/exact_fit.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="1000" padding="16"}
:::static
import afield.math.functions.Functions
import afield.math.autodiff.FnGradientMode

with(Functions) {
    val target = cos(2) * sin(1.5, amplitude = 0.8, offset = 0.2)
    val seed = cos(1.9) * sin(1.3, amplitude = 1.0)

    val fd = fitGradient(target, seed, iterations = 400, lr = 0.05)
    val exact = fitGradient(target, seed, iterations = 400, lr = 0.05, gradient = FnGradientMode.EXACT)

    // The exact path never trusts itself: it re-checks its own interpretation against Fn.eval on the
    // loss grid before switching over. Ask it why a piecewise oscillator is refused.
    val refusal = exactFitRefusal(target, valueNoise(3L, 2.0, 0.8), Functions.Domain.DEFAULT)
:::fold draw target, fit and both loss trajectories
    plot(target, channel = "1 target", title = "target   cos(2) * sin(1.5)")
    plot(exact.fitted, channel = "2 fitted", title = "fitted, exact reverse-mode gradients")
    showSignals(
        "finite differences" to fd.losses,
        "exact reverse mode" to exact.losses,
        channel = "3 loss",
        title = "RMSE per Adam step - same optimiser, different gradient",
        xTitle = "step", yTitle = "RMSE"
    )
    // The refusal names every differentiable op, which is one ~700-character line. Left unwrapped it
    // sets the width of the whole capture — the plots above end up small inside a very wide, mostly
    // empty frame. Wrap it on comma boundaries so the figure is sized by its plots, not by its prose.
    fun wrap(text: String, at: Int = 96): String {
        val out = StringBuilder()
        var column = 0
        for ((i, piece) in text.split(", ").withIndex()) {
            val token = if (i == 0) piece else ", $piece"
            if (column + token.length > at) { out.append(",\n     ").append(piece); column = 5 + piece.length }
            else { out.append(token); column += token.length }
        }
        return out.toString()
    }
    val numbers =
        "finite differences: RMSE " + fd.initialError + " -> " + fd.finalError + " in " + fd.evaluations + " loss evaluations\n" +
        "exact reverse mode: RMSE " + exact.initialError + " -> " + exact.finalError + " in " + exact.evaluations + " loss evaluations\n" +
        "a valueNoise seed is refused, with a reason:\n  " + wrap(refusal ?: "(none)")
    markdown("4 numbers", """
        ~~~
$numbers
        ~~~
    """)
:::endfold
}
```

![The target signal, a visually indistinguishable fitted signal, and two overlapping RMSE-versus-step curves that both fall from 0.36 to under 0.015](assets/autodiff_examples/exact_fit.png)

The exact run reaches a lower error with an eighth of the loss evaluations. It is somewhat faster,
though not eight times faster, because recording the derivative costs time too. It also leaves no
`fdStep` to tune, and it needs one sweep per step however many parameters there are, where finite
differences need two evaluations per parameter.

The last line of the figure shows a function being refused. Only 41<!--count:differentiableFnOpsOnExamplesPage-->
of `OpRegistry`'s 127<!--count:canonicalFnOpsOnExamplesPage--> canonical ops have a derivative; the
burst and pattern pulse generators, the seeded noise generators, the table-backed interpolants and the windowed
numeric operators do not. `FnGradientMode.EXACT` throws with the reason, `FnGradientMode.AUTO` falls
back to finite differences, and `FnFitRun.usedExactGradient` tells you which happened.

An op can be differentiated when its formula is stored in the graph. One built with
`Fn.mapY { … }` cannot, because `mapY` stores a Kotlin lambda that Field cannot look inside. So
`abs` is differentiable, while a `mapY { … }` of your own is refused however simple it is.

At its corner at zero, `abs` reports a derivative of `0`, halfway between the slopes on either
side. A central difference reports the same value there, so the two methods agree at the corner too.

A differentiable starting function can still fit badly. Swap the seed above for
`cos(1.9).abs() * sin(1.3, amplitude = 1.0)` and the exact path runs, but the error levels off
around 0.14, where the smooth seed reached about 0.01, and more iterations barely help. The `abs`
creates a local minimum, and gradient descent cannot climb out of one.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/autodiff_examples/abs_seed.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="900" padding="16"}

    // second of these was refused outright, with `mapY` named as the culprit.
    val kinked = cos(1.9).abs() * sin(1.3, amplitude = 1.0)

    val fd = fitGradient(target, kinked, iterations = 400, lr = 0.05)
    val exact = fitGradient(target, kinked, iterations = 400, lr = 0.05, gradient = FnGradientMode.EXACT)
:::fold plot the seed, the fit and both loss curves

## A packing that descends instead of relaxing

Circle packing is usually written as a relaxation loop: look for overlaps, nudge them apart, repeat.
Here it is written as a loss and minimized instead. The overlap of two discs is
`relu(r₁ + r₂ − distance)²`, zero while they are apart and growing quadratically once they overlap.
The walls work the same way. Every term is differentiable, so L-BFGS can minimize the whole thing.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/autodiff_examples/packing.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="620" padding="16"}
:::static

val boxWidth = 340.0
val boxHeight = 250.0
val packing = packCircles(radii, boxWidth, boxHeight, rngSeed = 5L)

// run.initialX is the seeded scatter the descent actually started from, so "before" is not a re-roll.
val before = radii.indices.map {
    PackedCircle(vec(packing.run.initialX[2 * it], packing.run.initialX[2 * it + 1]), radii[it])
}
:::fold draw both states in one shared window
fun frame() = fline {
    moveTo(0.0, 0.0); lineTo(boxWidth, 0.0); lineTo(boxWidth, boxHeight); lineTo(0.0, boxHeight)
    close(); color = vec(0.36, 0.44, 0.56, 0.7); thickness = 1.2
}
fun rings(circles: List<PackedCircle>, r: Double, g: Double, b: Double) = circles.map {
    it.toFLine(52).apply { color = vec(r, g, b, 0.95); thickness = 1.8 }
}
fun worstOverlapOf(circles: List<PackedCircle>): Double {
    var worst = 0.0
    for (i in circles.indices) for (j in i + 1 until circles.size) {
        val d = kotlin.math.hypot(
            (circles[i].centre.x - circles[j].centre.x).toDouble(),
            (circles[i].centre.y - circles[j].centre.y).toDouble()
        )
        worst = kotlin.math.max(worst, circles[i].radius + circles[j].radius - d)
    }
    return worst
}
showPlaneGrid(
    "before\nseeded scatter, worst overlap " + worstOverlapOf(before) + " units" to
        (rings(before, 0.52, 0.58, 0.72) + frame()),
    "after\n" + packing.run.iterations + " L-BFGS iterations, worst overlap " + packing.worstOverlap + " units" to
        (rings(packing.circles, 0.42, 0.86, 0.62) + frame()),
    channel = "1 packing", columns = 2, cellWidth = 380,
    window = Rect(-20.0, -20.0, boxWidth + 40.0, boxHeight + 40.0)
)
:::endfold
"worst pairwise overlap " + worstOverlapOf(before) + " -> " + packing.worstOverlap + " units\n" +
"worst escape beyond the wall: " + packing.worstEscape + " units\n" +
"loss " + packing.run.initialValue + " -> " + packing.run.value +
" in " + packing.run.iterations + " iterations (" + packing.run.reason + ")"
```

![Two panels sharing a frame: on the left a dozen circles of mixed sizes scattered and heavily overlapping inside a rectangle, on the right the same circles nested tightly against each other and the walls with no visible interpenetration](assets/autodiff_examples/packing.png)

A little overlap remains, because a gentle pull toward the centre works against the overlap term and
the result is where the two balance. Set `pullWeight` to `0.0` and the overlap goes, and so does the
compactness. The halfway derivative at a corner, described for `abs` above, matters here: when two
discs just touch, the discs settle into contact instead of bouncing in and out of it.

# Differentiating Functions

Field computes exact derivatives of the code you write, by automatic differentiation. Reverse mode
over `Double` gives gradients, second-order forward mode gives curvature, and SGD, Adam and L-BFGS
minimize using either. An `Fn` built from stdlib parts can be differentiated too, with respect to
its own numeric parameters.

## One expression, three ways of differentiating it

`AD` is a `Double` that remembers how it was made. Arithmetic on it appends to a tape; a single
backward sweep reads off every derivative at once. `grad { }` returns a function, so you can hand it
straight to an optimizer.

`Dual2` works the other way around, carrying a value with its first and second derivatives
`(v, v', v'')` along a single direction. Use it when there is one input and many outputs; it is also
what makes `hessian` exact. The second derivative comes with the forward pass, so all three curves
below come from one sweep.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/autodiff_examples/derivatives.png" wait="2.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="600" padding="16"}
:::static
// The same expression, differentiated by a tape sweep, by a Taylor number, and by a central
// difference. If any two of them disagree, one of them is wrong.
val xs = (0..300).map { it / 300.0 * 2.0 - 1.0 }
val taylor = xs.map { x -> taylor2(x) { u -> exp(-u * u) * sin(6.0 * u) } }
val reverse = xs.map { x -> derivative(x) { u -> exp(-u * u) * sin(6.0 * u) } }
val oracle = xs.map { x ->
    val plain = { u: Double -> kotlin.math.exp(-u * u) * kotlin.math.sin(6.0 * u) }
    (plain(x + 1e-6) - plain(x - 1e-6)) / 2e-6
}

// The exact Hessian of Rosenbrock: one Dual2 pass gives vT H v, and polarisation recovers the
// off-diagonals. Not a finite difference of a gradient.
val h = hessian(doubleArrayOf(-1.2, 1.0)) { p -> (1.0 - p[0]).sq() + 100.0 * (p[1] - p[0].sq()).sq() }
val g = grad { p: List<AD> -> (1.0 - p[0]).sq() + 100.0 * (p[1] - p[0].sq()).sq() }
:::fold draw the three orders and report the agreement
showSignals(
    "f" to taylor.map { it.value },
    "f' (reverse mode)" to reverse,
    "f'' (forward mode)" to taylor.map { it.second },
    x = xs,
    title = "exp(-x^2)*sin(6x), its slope and its curvature - one sweep, three orders",
    xTitle = "x"
)
val worstPair = xs.indices.maxOf { kotlin.math.abs(taylor[it].first - reverse[it]) }
val worstOracle = xs.indices.maxOf { kotlin.math.abs(reverse[it] - oracle[it]) }
val agreement =
    "grad Rosenbrock at (-1.2, 1.0) = " + g(doubleArrayOf(-1.2, 1.0)).toList() + "\n" +
    "exact Hessian there            = [[" + h[0][0] + ", " + h[0][1] + "], [" + h[1][0] + ", " + h[1][1] + "]]\n" +
    "forward vs reverse f', worst of 301 samples: " + worstPair + "\n" +
    "reverse vs central difference,  worst of 301: " + worstOracle
markdown("agreement", """
    ~~~
$agreement
    ~~~
""")
:::endfold
```

    showSignals(
        "finite differences" to fd.losses,
        "exact reverse mode" to exact.losses,
        channel = "3 loss",
        title = "RMSE per Adam step - same optimiser, different gradient",
        xTitle = "step", yTitle = "RMSE"
    )
    // The refusal names every differentiable op, which is one ~700-character line. Left unwrapped it
    // sets the width of the whole capture — the plots above end up small inside a very wide, mostly
    // empty frame. Wrap it on comma boundaries so the figure is sized by its plots, not by its prose.
    fun wrap(text: String, at: Int = 96): String {
        val out = StringBuilder()
        var column = 0
        for ((i, piece) in text.split(", ").withIndex()) {
            val token = if (i == 0) piece else ", $piece"
            if (column + token.length > at) { out.append(",\n     ").append(piece); column = 5 + piece.length }
            else { out.append(token); column += token.length }
        }
        return out.toString()
    }
    val numbers =
        "finite differences: RMSE " + fd.initialError + " -> " + fd.finalError + " in " + fd.evaluations + " loss evaluations\n" +
        "exact reverse mode: RMSE " + exact.initialError + " -> " + exact.finalError + " in " + exact.evaluations + " loss evaluations\n" +
        "a valueNoise seed is refused, with a reason:\n  " + wrap(refusal ?: "(none)")
    markdown("4 numbers", """
        ~~~
$numbers
        ~~~
    """)
:::endfold
}

![The target signal, a visually indistinguishable fitted signal, and two overlapping RMSE-versus-step curves that both fall from 0.36 to under 0.015](assets/autodiff_examples/exact_fit.png)

The exact run reaches a lower error with an eighth of the loss evaluations. It is somewhat faster,
though not eight times faster, because recording the derivative costs time too. It also leaves no
`fdStep` to tune, and it needs one sweep per step however many parameters there are, where finite
differences need two evaluations per parameter.

The last line of the figure shows a function being refused. Only 41<!--count:differentiableFnOpsOnExamplesPage-->
of `OpRegistry`'s 127<!--count:canonicalFnOpsOnExamplesPage--> canonical ops have a derivative; the
burst and pattern pulse generators, the seeded noise generators, the table-backed interpolants and the windowed
numeric operators do not. `FnGradientMode.EXACT` throws with the reason, `FnGradientMode.AUTO` falls
back to finite differences, and `FnFitRun.usedExactGradient` tells you which happened.

An op can be differentiated when its formula is stored in the graph. One built with
`Fn.mapY { … }` cannot, because `mapY` stores a Kotlin lambda that Field cannot look inside. So
`abs` is differentiable, while a `mapY { … }` of your own is refused however simple it is.

At its corner at zero, `abs` reports a derivative of `0`, halfway between the slopes on either
side. A central difference reports the same value there, so the two methods agree at the corner too.

A differentiable starting function can still fit badly. Swap the seed above for
`cos(1.9).abs() * sin(1.3, amplitude = 1.0)` and the exact path runs, but the error levels off
around 0.14, where the smooth seed reached about 0.01, and more iterations barely help. The `abs`
creates a local minimum, and gradient descent cannot climb out of one.

## Inverse kinematics on a chain of links

The position of the tip of a chain of links is a running sum of joint angles and link vectors, which
is differentiable. So finding the joint angles that put the tip on a target is L-BFGS on
`|tip - target|²`, and the result is an `FLine` you can draw.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/autodiff_examples/inverse_kinematics.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="560" padding="16"}

## A packing that descends instead of relaxing

Circle packing is usually written as a relaxation loop: look for overlaps, nudge them apart, repeat.
Here it is written as a loss and minimized instead. The overlap of two discs is
`relu(r₁ + r₂ − distance)²`, zero while they are apart and growing quadratically once they overlap.
The walls work the same way. Every term is differentiable, so L-BFGS can minimize the whole thing.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/autodiff_examples/packing.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="620" padding="16"}
:::static
val radii = doubleArrayOf(38.0, 32.0, 30.0, 26.0, 24.0, 22.0, 20.0, 18.0, 16.0, 14.0, 12.0, 10.0)
val boxWidth = 340.0
val boxHeight = 250.0
val packing = packCircles(radii, boxWidth, boxHeight, rngSeed = 5L)

// run.initialX is the seeded scatter the descent actually started from, so "before" is not a re-roll.
val before = radii.indices.map {
    PackedCircle(vec(packing.run.initialX[2 * it], packing.run.initialX[2 * it + 1]), radii[it])
}
:::fold draw both states in one shared window
fun frame() = fline {
    rect(0.0, 0.0, boxWidth, boxHeight); color = vec(0.36, 0.44, 0.56, 0.7); thickness = 1.2
}
fun rings(circles: List<PackedCircle>, r: Double, g: Double, b: Double) = circles.map {
    it.toFLine(52).apply { color = vec(r, g, b, 0.95); thickness = 1.8 }
}
fun worstOverlapOf(circles: List<PackedCircle>): Double {
    var worst = 0.0
    for (i in circles.indices) for (j in i + 1 until circles.size) {
        val d = kotlin.math.hypot(
            (circles[i].centre.x - circles[j].centre.x).toDouble(),
            (circles[i].centre.y - circles[j].centre.y).toDouble()
        )
        worst = kotlin.math.max(worst, circles[i].radius + circles[j].radius - d)
    }
    return worst
}
showPlaneGrid(
    "before\nseeded scatter, worst overlap " + worstOverlapOf(before) + " units" to
        (rings(before, 0.52, 0.58, 0.72) + frame()),
    "after\n" + packing.run.iterations + " L-BFGS iterations, worst overlap " + packing.worstOverlap + " units" to
        (rings(packing.circles, 0.42, 0.86, 0.62) + frame()),
    channel = "1 packing", columns = 2, cellWidth = 380,
    window = Rect(-20.0, -20.0, boxWidth + 40.0, boxHeight + 40.0)
)
:::endfold
"worst pairwise overlap " + worstOverlapOf(before) + " -> " + packing.worstOverlap + " units\n" +
"worst escape beyond the wall: " + packing.worstEscape + " units\n" +
"loss " + packing.run.initialValue + " -> " + packing.run.value +
" in " + packing.run.iterations + " iterations (" + packing.run.reason + ")"
```

![Two panels sharing a frame: on the left a dozen circles of mixed sizes scattered and heavily overlapping inside a rectangle, on the right the same circles nested tightly against each other and the walls with no visible interpenetration](assets/autodiff_examples/packing.png)

A little overlap remains, because a gentle pull toward the centre works against the overlap term and
the result is where the two balance. Set `pullWeight` to `0.0` and the overlap goes, and so does the
compactness. The halfway derivative at a corner, described for `abs` above, matters here: when two
discs just touch, the discs settle into contact instead of bouncing in and out of it.

# Drawn Strokes Become Paint

Every pen stroke on the drawing layer is a line of points, and a tablet pen records how hard it was
pressed at each one. `notation` reads both back, and `PaintCanvas` drags a simulated oil brush along
the points, pressing as hard as the pen did. The paint is mixed from tube colours, stays wet, smears
into whatever wet paint it crosses, and dries over simulated hours.

This meadow is 560 strokes on the drawing, painted back to front onto a red-ground oil canvas: a sky
of long sweeps that warm from cobalt to Naples yellow, clouds scumbled in lead white, a field, then
grass flicked up from the root so each blade thins as the pen lifts, and poppies on top. The grass
goes into the field paint before it is dry and drags some of it along.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/chain_drawn_paint/meadow.png" wait="40" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="18" timeout="300" requires="paint" name="chain-drawn-paint-meadow" embed=true alt="An oil painting of a meadow at evening on a canvas with a visible weave. Below a thin blue-green band of distant hills, a green and ochre field is crowded with hundreds of tapering blades of grass, short and fine near the horizon and taller and broader towards the bottom, darkening to umber at the foot. Scattered through the grass are sixty red poppies, small in the distance and larger in front."}

val Y = region.y

    for (i in 0 until 18) stroke(sweep(r(-160.0, 0.0), 20.0 + i * 26 + r(-6.0, 6.0), 1760.0, r(-10.0, 10.0)),   // sky
        name = "sky $i", pressure = { 0.5 + 0.5 * sin(PI * it) })
    for (c in 0 until 5) {                                                                                  // clouds
        val cx = r(150.0, 1350.0); val cy = r(90.0, 300.0)
        for (k in 0 until 7) stroke(sweep(cx + r(-120.0, 80.0), cy + r(-35.0, 25.0), r(80.0, 220.0), 4.0),
            name = "cloud $c.$k", pressure = { 0.2 + 0.8 * sin(PI * it) })

    for (i in 0 until 22) stroke(sweep(-80.0, 540.0 + i * 22, 1760.0),                                       // the field
        name = "field $i", pressure = { 0.7 + 0.3 * sin(PI * it) })
    for (i in 0 until 420) {                                                                                // grass
        val y = r(560.0, 1000.0); val d = (y - 540) / 460; val x = r(-20.0, 1620.0)
        val h = r(40.0, 120.0) + 300 * d * d; val lean = r(-0.3, 0.5) * h

val field = canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width = 50.0)
named("field").forEachIndexed { i, s ->
    val t = i / 21.0
    paint(s, field.load(mapOf("green earth" to 2.0, "yellow ochre" to 2.0 * (1 - t), "raw umber" to 1.5 * t, "lead white" to 1.0 * (1 - t)), wipe = 0.5))

canvas.wait(40.0)   // let the field set a little before the grass goes into it
val grass = canvas.brush(BrushKind.Round, width = 10.0)
val greens = [mapOf("viridian" to 1.0, "yellow ochre" to 1.5), mapOf("green earth" to 2.0, "chrome yellow" to 1.0),
    mapOf("viridian" to 1.0, "raw umber" to 1.0), mapOf("yellow ochre" to 2.0, "lead white" to 1.0),
    mapOf("Prussian blue" to 0.2, "chrome yellow" to 2.0), mapOf("Naples yellow" to 2.0, "green earth" to 1.0)]
named("grass").sortedBy { it.start!!.y }.forEachIndexed { i, s -> paint(s, grass.load(greens[i % greens.size], wipe = 0.5), 0.4 + 0.6 * depth(s), shake = 0.6) }

named("poppy").sortedBy { it.start!!.y }.forEach { s -> paint(s, poppy.load(mapOf("vermilion" to 3.0, "cadmium red" to 1.0, "lead white" to 0.2), wipe = 0.9), 0.3 + 0.7 * depth(s)) }

canvas.glaze(rgb(0.6, 0.45, 0.2), coats = 0.12)   // a thin warm varnish over the whole thing

## Three strokes, with pressure

`notation { stroke(...) }` writes a stroke into the drawing. Its `pressure` argument gives the pen
pressure, 0 to 1, as a function of how far along the stroke the pen is. This box draws three: a wave
named `S` that is pressed hardest in the middle, a `sweep` that starts hard and lifts off, and a
`loop` that starts light and bears down as it curls in to its end. It reads them back and plots the
pressure along each. The figure shows the drawing on the left and the box with its output on the
right:

`pressures` is the list Excalidraw keeps, one value per point. A pen records points closer together
where it moves slowly, so that list is not evenly spaced along the stroke. `pressuresAlong(n)` gives
the pressure at `n` points evenly spaced by distance, which is what a brush wants. A stroke drawn
with a mouse has no pressure, and both lists are empty.

## Painted, pressing as the pen did

`PaintCanvas(view = ...)` stretches a rectangle of drawing coordinates over the whole canvas, so the
strokes need no conversion: `toFLine()` gives each one in drawing coordinates, and the drawing and
the canvas both have y growing downwards. A brush's `swell` is a list of pressure multipliers along
the stroke, so with the base `pressure` at 1, `swell = pressuresAlong(64)` presses the brush as the
pen pressed.

The top row is painted that way. In the middle row the pen's pressure is squared first, and in the
bottom row the brush is held at one even pressure:

fun lower(s: Mark, dy: Double) = FLine().also { f -> s.points.forEachIndexed { k, p -> if (k == 0) f.moveTo(p.x, p.y + dy) else f.lineTo(p.x, p.y + dy) } }

    canvas.stroke(s.toFLine(), brush, pressure = 1.0..1.0, swell = pen)
    brush.load(colours[i % 3], wipe = 1.0)
    canvas.stroke(lower(s, 360.0), brush, pressure = 1.0..1.0, swell = pen.map { it * it })
    brush.load(colours[i % 3], wipe = 1.0)
    canvas.stroke(lower(s, 720.0), brush, pressure = 0.6..0.6)

A round brush pressed as lightly as it goes still lays a band about a third of its full width, so
painting straight from the pen gives a narrower range than the pen recorded. Squaring the pressure
spreads the light end out: a stroke at half pressure paints at a quarter, and the lightest parts of
a stroke thin to a few bristles. Any function of the pressure works here, and a curve like this one
is what a drawing program's pressure setting is.

## Strokes that cross

Wet paint mixes with what is on the canvas the way pigment does, not the way light does. Here four
yellow and red pairs of bands are each crossed by one stroke. In the first, ultramarine goes straight
across the wet bands and turns green over the yellow and dark over the red. In the second the same
blue crosses the same bands after `dry()`, and sits on top of them as a transparent film. In the
third a clean, dry hog-hair brush with no paint of its own is dragged through: it picks up the
yellow and smears it down into the red. In the fourth a clean badger blender does the same more
softly:

the time of an average paint and bone black in more than twice. `dry()` waits until every stroke is
touch-dry. Rendering does not change the canvas, so the strokes are still wet for the next one.

# Drawn Strokes Become Paint

Every pen stroke on the drawing layer is a line of points, and a tablet pen records how hard it was
pressed at each one. `notation` reads both back, and `PaintCanvas` drags a simulated oil brush along
the points, pressing as hard as the pen did. The paint is mixed from tube colours, stays wet, smears
into whatever wet paint it crosses, and dries over simulated hours.

of long sweeps that warm from cobalt to Naples yellow, clouds scumbled in lead white, a field, then
grass flicked up from the root so each blade thins as the pen lifts, and poppies on top. The grass
goes into the field paint before it is dry and drags some of it along.

The strokes are drawn by code here, from a seeded random hand, so that the page rebuilds the same
way. The painting part reads them back from a region of the drawing, `notation.strokes.filter {
it.bounds.intersects(region) }`, so strokes you draw in that region with the pen are painted too.

## Three strokes, with pressure

`notation { stroke(...) }` writes a stroke into the drawing. Its `pressure` argument gives the pen
pressure, 0 to 1, as a function of how far along the stroke the pen is. This box draws three: a wave
named `S` that is pressed hardest in the middle, a `sweep` that starts hard and lifts off, and a
`loop` that starts light and bears down as it curls in to its end. It reads them back and plots the
pressure along each. The figure shows the drawing on the left and the box with its output on the
right:

// (0..1) as a function of how far along the stroke the pen is. Running it again replaces them.

    stroke(FLine().moveTo(80, 300).cubicTo(200, 60, 330, 420, 420, 140), name = "S",
        pressure = { 0.15 + 0.85 * sin(PI * it) })
    stroke(FLine().moveTo(470, 110).cubicTo(560, 300, 700, 330, 820, 180), name = "sweep",

```

`pressures` is the list Excalidraw keeps, one value per point. A pen records points closer together
where it moves slowly, so that list is not evenly spaced along the stroke. `pressuresAlong(n)` gives
the pressure at `n` points evenly spaced by distance, which is what a brush wants. A stroke drawn
with a mouse has no pressure, and both lists are empty.

## Painted, pressing as the pen did

`PaintCanvas(view = ...)` stretches a rectangle of drawing coordinates over the whole canvas, so the
strokes need no conversion: `toFLine()` gives each one in drawing coordinates, and the drawing and
the canvas both have y growing downwards. A brush's `swell` is a list of pressure multipliers along
the stroke, so with the base `pressure` at 1, `swell = pressuresAlong(64)` presses the brush as the
pen pressed.

The top row is painted that way. In the middle row the pen's pressure is squared first, and in the
bottom row the brush is held at one even pressure:

In the middle row the same changes are much stronger: the wave's ends and the arc's tail thin to a line of bristle marks, and the spiral's outer curve is a thin trail. In the bottom row all three are bands of one even width."}

// pressing as the pen did; the pen's pressure squared, so light strokes go lighter; one even pressure.
val region = Rect(40.0, 40.0, 1040.0, 400.0)
val strokes = notation.strokes.filter { it.bounds.intersects(region) }
val colours = [mapOf("ultramarine blue" to 2.0, "bone black" to 0.3), mapOf("vermilion" to 1.0), mapOf("viridian" to 1.0, "chrome yellow" to 0.6)]
val canvas = PaintCanvas(900, aspect = 0.9, view = Rect(40.0, 40.0, 1000.0, 1110.0))
val brush = canvas.brush(BrushKind.Round, width = 70.0)
fun lower(s: Mark, dy: Double) = s.toFLine() + vec(0.0, dy)
strokes.forEachIndexed { i, s ->
    val pen = s.pressuresAlong(64)
    brush.load(colours[i % 3], wipe = 1.0)
    canvas.stroke(s.toFLine(), brush, pressure = 1.0..1.0, swell = pen)
    brush.load(colours[i % 3], wipe = 1.0)
    canvas.stroke(lower(s, 360.0), brush, pressure = 1.0..1.0, swell = pen.map { it * it })
    brush.load(colours[i % 3], wipe = 1.0)
    canvas.stroke(lower(s, 720.0), brush, pressure = 0.6..0.6)
}
display("main", canvas.png())
notation.clear()   // take the strokes down so they do not lie over the picture
```

A round brush pressed as lightly as it goes still lays a band about a third of its full width, so
painting straight from the pen gives a narrower range than the pen recorded. Squaring the pressure
spreads the light end out: a stroke at half pressure paints at a quarter, and the lightest parts of
a stroke thin to a few bristles. Any function of the pressure works here, and a curve like this one
is what a drawing program's pressure setting is.

## Strokes that cross

Wet paint mixes with what is on the canvas the way pigment does, not the way light does. Here four
yellow and red pairs of bands are each crossed by one stroke. In the first, ultramarine goes straight
across the wet bands and turns green over the yellow and dark over the red. In the second the same
blue crosses the same bands after `dry()`, and sits on top of them as a transparent film. In the
third a clean, dry hog-hair brush with no paint of its own is dragged through: it picks up the
yellow and smears it down into the red. In the fourth a clean badger blender does the same more
softly:

How fast a stroke dries depends on how thick it is and on its paint: lead white dries in about half
the time of an average paint and bone black in more than twice. `dry()` waits until every stroke is
touch-dry. Rendering does not change the canvas, so the strokes are still wet for the next one.

## In pencil

`canvas.draw(line, pencil, pressure = ...)` takes the same kind of list, a pressure at evenly spaced

# Flow Matching

`flowMatch` fits a velocity field that carries one cloud of points onto another. Integrating that
field from `t = 0` to `t = 1` moves the first distribution onto the second, and stopping part-way
gives every stage in between. The input is a few hundred to a few thousand points in two or three
dimensions — a sampled `FLine` with noise around it is the usual case — and training takes about a
second.

The method is short enough to state completely. Pick a point `x0` from where you are starting and a
point `x1` from where you want to end up, and declare that the straight line between them is the
path a particle should take: at time `t` it sits at `xt = (1-t)·x0 + t·x1` travelling at `x1 - x0`.
Then fit a network `v(x, t)` to that velocity by least squares over many random `(x0, x1, t)`
triples. No two straight lines agree where they cross, so the fit cannot reproduce any one of them;
it converges to the average velocity through each point at each time, and integrating that average
transports the whole starting distribution onto the whole target one. The loss is a regression mean
squared error, so there is no adversary and nothing to diverge.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
:::static
val field = flowMatch(myCloud)                 // from a Gaussian: a generator
val fresh = field.sample(500)                  // new points shaped like myCloud
val threads = field.paths(80)                  // the trajectories, as FLines

val morph = flowMatch(to = cloudB, from = cloudA)
val halfway = morph.transport(cloudA, to = 0.5) // a real intermediate distribution
```

## Sampling new points shaped like a cloud

With no `from` cloud the particles start from a standard Gaussian, which makes the result a
generator: `sample` draws points that were not in the training data but are shaped like it.

The panels are the target cloud with the generated one on top of it, then the trajectories that
produced it. Each trajectory starts somewhere in the Gaussian blur at the centre and ends on the
ring.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/flow_matching/ring.png" wait="2.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="480" padding="16"}

fun cloud(points: List<Vec3>, size: Double, c: Vec4, shift: Vec3 = vec(0, 0, 0)): FLine {
    val f = FLine()
    points.forEach { f.moveTo(it + shift) }
    f.pointed = true
    f.pointSize = size
    f.color = c
    return f
}

val target = (0 until 500).map {
    val a = random() * 2 * PI
    vec(100 * cos(a), 100 * sin(a), 0.0)
}

val field = flowMatch(target, options = FlowMatchOptions(steps = 6000, seed = 11))
val samples = field.sample(500, seed = 12)

// The ring's radius is a single number, so the fit can be stated rather than eyeballed.
val radii = samples.map { hypot(it.x.toDouble(), it.y.toDouble()) }
val mean = radii.average()
val sd = sqrt(radii.sumOf { (it - mean) * (it - mean) } / radii.size)

val threads = field.paths(80, steps = 48, seed = 13).map {
    it.color = vec(0.44, 0.83, 0.78, 0.55)
    it.thickness = 0.8
    it
} + vec(330, 0, 0)

        // Target underneath at a larger point size, so it shows as a halo where the two agree.
        cloud(target, 3.0, vec(0.55, 0.55, 0.62, 0.9)),
        cloud(samples, 1.4, vec(0.44, 0.83, 0.78, 1.0)),

markdown("fit", """
    ~~~
generated radius   ${"%.1f".format(mean)} +/- ${"%.1f".format(sd)}   (target: 100)
chamfer to target  ${"%.2f".format(chamferDistance(samples, target))}
training loss      ${"%.4f".format(field.loss(200))} over ${field.parameterCount} parameters

:::endfold

![Left: a ring of grey points with cyan generated points lying on top of it. Right: eighty thin trajectories fanning out from a dense knot at the centre to the circumference of a circle](assets/flow_matching/ring.png)

The training loss settles near 1.3 and stays there, because most of it is irreducible. Where paths
cross, the field can only predict their average, and that residual is a property of the problem
rather than of the fit. Loss is therefore not a quality measure here; compare samples instead, with
`chamferDistance` or by looking.

Two conventions are chosen for you. Training happens in a centred, isotropically scaled frame, since
a Gaussian source has to be commensurate with the data and `FLine` coordinates are usually in the
hundreds; the scaling is one factor rather than one per axis, so a shape keeps its aspect ratio, and
everything you pass in and get back is in your own coordinates. And 2D against 3D is decided by the
data rather than by an argument: a cloud whose `z` never varies trains as a two-dimensional problem
and its samples come back on that same plane. `FlowMatchOptions.dimension` overrides that.

## Moving one cloud onto another

Given a `from` cloud the field becomes a map between two shapes, and `transport` can stop at any
`t`. `transport(cloudA, to = 0.5)` is a genuine intermediate distribution rather than a vertex-wise
average of two point lists.

When something upstream already knows which point goes where — a shared arc coordinate along two
curves, say — `FlowCoupling.PAIRED` uses that correspondence instead of guessing one. The target
velocity then becomes a function of `(x, t)` rather than an average over crossing paths, the loss
floor drops from the data's variance to near zero, and the result can be graded point by point: this
point was supposed to land there, and it landed here.

Doing that exposes a limit that matters when choosing the source shape. Integrating a velocity field
is a continuous invertible map, so it can deform a curve but cannot tear a loop open or join two
strands. Asking a straight segment to become a closed ring pulls the segment's two ends to the same
target point, and their paths have to cross. The left panel gives the closed target a closed source;
the right panel gives it a segment, at identical settings.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/flow_matching/topology.png" wait="2.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="520" padding="16"}
:::static
val n = 300

// Both curves are sampled in order of their own arc coordinate, so point i at one end is the same
// material point as point i at the other. That is what PAIRED needs.
fun closed(radius: Double): List<Vec3> = (0 until n).map {
    val s = it / (n - 1.0)
    vec(radius * cos(2 * PI * s), radius * sin(2 * PI * s), 0.0)
}

val target = closed(100.0)
val circleSource = closed(30.0)
val segmentSource = (0 until n).map { vec(200 * (it / (n - 1.0) - 0.5), -150.0, 0.0) }

val options = FlowMatchOptions(steps = 6000, seed = 11, coupling = FlowCoupling.PAIRED)
val fromCircle = flowMatch(target, circleSource, options = options)
val fromSegment = flowMatch(target, segmentSource, options = options)

fun miss(field: FlowMatchField, source: List<Vec3>): Double {
    val landed = field.transport(source, steps = 64)
    return landed.indices.sumOf { (landed[it] - target[it]).length().toDouble() } / n
}
:::fold draw the two morphs side by side and report where each point landed
fun asClosed(points: List<Vec3>, c: Vec4, t: Double): FLine = fline {
    points.forEachIndexed { i, p -> if (i == 0) moveTo(p) else lineTo(p) }
    color = c
    thickness = t
}

// Grey is the target, purple the source at t = 0, cyan the flow between them -- the same three
// roles, in the same three colours, as every other figure on this page. The target is drawn even
// though the t = 1 stage lands on top of it, because otherwise there is nothing to judge against.
fun stages(field: FlowMatchField, source: List<Vec3>): List<FLine> =
    [
        asClosed(target, vec(0.45, 0.45, 0.52, 0.9), 3.0),
        asClosed(source, vec(0.6, 0.42, 0.85, 1.0), 1.8),
    ] + [0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0].map {
        asClosed(field.transport(source, to = it, steps = 48), vec(0.44, 0.83, 0.78, 0.9), 1.2)
    }

lines(
    stages(fromCircle, circleSource) + (stages(fromSegment, segmentSource) + vec(260, 0, 0)),
    w = 1000.0, h = 500.0, fitToSize = true,
)
markdown("miss", """
    ~~~
closed source (circle -> ring)    mean landing error ${"%.2f".format(miss(fromCircle, circleSource))}
open source   (segment -> ring)   mean landing error ${"%.2f".format(miss(fromSegment, segmentSource))}
    ~~~
""")
:::endfold
```

![Left: a small purple circle with four cyan curves stepping outward from it, the outermost sitting on a thick grey target ring. Right: a purple straight line beside the same grey target ring, with cyan curves that cross themselves and never settle onto it](assets/flow_matching/topology.png)

The numbers under the figure are roughly 0.3 units against 67 on a radius-100 ring. The topology
mismatch costs more than every other setting on this page combined, and training longer does not
help: a longer run only fits the crossing-averaged velocity more precisely. Give a closed target a closed source, an open target an open one.

`FlowCoupling` has a third option, `MINIBATCH_OT`, which pairs points within each batch by solving
the assignment that minimises total squared travel. It cuts the training loss by about ten times
because it removes most of the crossing. It does not follow that the samples improve: on the ring
above it is slightly worse than independent pairing, since it only ever sees one batch of the cloud
at a time. `INDEPENDENT` is the default.

## Width along the curve

A centreline discards what the cloud says about its own spread. If the source strand is given a
constant transverse thickness and the target tube's thickness varies along its length, the field
learns both the bend and the change in width.

Here the source is a straight strand of constant width 9, and the target is a wiggling curve whose
width swells from 3 at the ends to 29 in the middle. The four panels are the source and three stages
of the flow.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/flow_matching/tube.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="560" padding="16"}
:::static
val n = 1200

// Each sample is (s along the curve, r across it), so source and target share a point identity.
val draws: List<Pair<Double, Double>> = (0 until n).map { Pair(random(), randomGaussian()) }

fun width(s: Double): Double = 3.0 + 26.0 * sin(PI * s) * sin(PI * s)
fun centre(s: Double): Vec3 = vec(240 * (s - 0.5), 70 * sin(3 * PI * s), 0.0)

// Unit normal of the centreline: the direction the width is measured along.
fun normal(s: Double): Vec3 {
    val dy = 70.0 * 3 * PI * cos(3 * PI * s)
    val len = hypot(240.0, dy)
    return vec(-dy / len, 240.0 / len, 0.0)
}

val source = draws.map { vec(240 * (it.first - 0.5), 150 + 9 * it.second, 0.0) }
val target = draws.map { (s, r) -> centre(s) + normal(s) * (width(s) * r) }

val field = flowMatch(
    target, source,
    options = FlowMatchOptions(steps = 8000, seed = 11, coupling = FlowCoupling.PAIRED),
)

// Transverse spread measured along the centreline normal, so it reports width rather than a blob
// radius that would also contain the travel along the curve.
fun transverseSd(points: List<Vec3>, from: Double, to: Double): Double {
    val picked = draws.indices.filter { draws[it].first >= from && draws[it].first < to }
    val offsets = picked.map {
        val s = draws[it].first
        val d = points[it] - centre(s)
        (d.x * normal(s).x + d.y * normal(s).y).toDouble()
    }
    return sqrt(offsets.sumOf { it * it } / offsets.size)
}

    ~~~
transverse width at t = 1, measured along the centreline normal

${rows.joinToString("\n")}

## Settings that change the result

A few of `FlowMatchOptions`'s fields account for most of the variation, and the first two have
defaults that may surprise you.

`activation` defaults to `leaky` rather than `tanh`. A velocity field has to keep growing away from
the data — near `t = 0` the right answer is roughly `-x`, without bound — and a saturating unit
cannot, so it bends the far field back on itself. On the ring above, `tanh` gives about four times
the radial spread of `leaky` or `relu` at equal cost, more than any other setting changes it.

`finalLearningRate` decays the rate linearly across the run, and defaults to doing so. RMSProp
rescales the gradient to roughly unit length, so a constant rate keeps taking same-sized steps
however close to the answer it already is, and the fit settles at a floor set by the rate. At a
constant rate, more steps can leave the result *further* from its target; with the decay, more
steps help, and the ring's radial spread drops from 9.2 to 3.6.

`steps` is then the quality knob worth reaching for first, and the dominant cost: roughly 0.08 ms
per step at the default batch, so 6000 steps is about half a second. `hidden` defaults to two layers
of 64 units, and widening it helps much less than training longer.

`FlowMatchField.losses` records every step, so a loss still falling at the end means the run was cut
short.

## Limits of the method

The field is a deformation, so it cannot change topology: no tearing a loop, no joining two strands,
no branching. Multiple curves can be carried by one field as long as each has its own source strand
of the same kind, and they will approach each other without crossing.

`sample` returns an unordered cloud. Recovering an `FLine` from one is a separate problem, which
`transport` sidesteps by moving points you already have and keeping their order.

There is no conditioning input: one field carries one distribution onto one other. And it is a small
model — two layers of 64 units suits a few thousand points in two or three dimensions and would not
suit an image.

The API is in [Machine learning](reference/machine-learning.md); `VectorMLP` there is the
multi-output regression head that `flowMatch` trains, which is usable on its own.

`FlowMatchField.export()` takes a trained field to the GPU as an unrolled GLSL forward pass, and
`mixtureSource` builds the matched-topology source a multi-component target needs. Both are on
[Particle rules that were trained](neural_particles.md), along with what the loss on this page does
and does not tell you.

See also [Stipple transport](stipple_transport.md), which carries a uniform
sheet onto a stippled image and animates between images with one network, trained in PyTorch and
queried from Field without Python.
