# Flow Matching

`flowMatch` fits a velocity field that carries one cloud of points onto another. Integrating that
field from `t = 0` to `t = 1` moves the first distribution onto the second, and stopping part-way
gives every stage in between. The input is a few hundred to a few thousand points in two or three
dimensions — a sampled `FLine` with noise around it is the usual case — and training takes about a
second.

The method is short enough to state completely. Pick a point `x0` from where you are starting and a
point `x1` from where you want to end up, and declare that the straight line between them is the
path a particle should take: at time `t` it sits at `xt = (1-t)·x0 + t·x1` travelling at `x1 - x0`.
Then fit a network `v(x, t)` to that velocity by least squares over many random `(x0, x1, t)`
triples. No two straight lines agree where they cross, so the fit cannot reproduce any one of them;
it converges to the average velocity through each point at each time, and integrating that average
transports the whole starting distribution onto the whole target one. The loss is a regression mean
squared error, so there is no adversary and nothing to diverge.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
:::static
val field = flowMatch(myCloud)                 // from a Gaussian: a generator
val fresh = field.sample(500)                  // new points shaped like myCloud
val threads = field.paths(80)                  // the trajectories, as FLines

val morph = flowMatch(to = cloudB, from = cloudA)
val halfway = morph.transport(cloudA, to = 0.5) // a real intermediate distribution
```

## Sampling new points shaped like a cloud

With no `from` cloud the particles start from a standard Gaussian, which makes the result a
generator: `sample` draws points that were not in the training data but are shaped like it.

The panels are the target cloud with the generated one on top of it, then the trajectories that
produced it. Each trajectory starts somewhere in the Gaussian blur at the centre and ends on the
ring.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/flow_matching/ring.png" wait="2.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="480" padding="16"}

    val f = FLine()
    points.forEach { f.moveTo(it + shift) }
    f.pointed = true
    f.pointSize = size
    f.color = c
    return f
}

val target = (0 until 500).map {
    val a = random() * 2 * PI
    vec(100 * cos(a), 100 * sin(a), 0.0)
}

val field = flowMatch(target, options = FlowMatchOptions(steps = 6000, seed = 11))
val samples = field.sample(500, seed = 12)

// The ring's radius is a single number, so the fit can be stated rather than eyeballed.
val radii = samples.map { hypot(it.x.toDouble(), it.y.toDouble()) }
val mean = radii.average()
val sd = sqrt(radii.sumOf { (it - mean) * (it - mean) } / radii.size)

    it.color = vec(0.44, 0.83, 0.78, 0.55)

The training loss settles near 1.3 and stays there, because most of it is irreducible. Where paths
cross, the field can only predict their average, and that residual is a property of the problem
rather than of the fit. Loss is therefore not a quality measure here; compare samples instead, with
`chamferDistance` or by looking.

Two conventions are chosen for you. Training happens in a centred, isotropically scaled frame, since
a Gaussian source has to be commensurate with the data and `FLine` coordinates are usually in the
hundreds; the scaling is one factor rather than one per axis, so a shape keeps its aspect ratio, and
everything you pass in and get back is in your own coordinates. And 2D against 3D is decided by the
data rather than by an argument: a cloud whose `z` never varies trains as a two-dimensional problem
and its samples come back on that same plane. `FlowMatchOptions.dimension` overrides that.

## Moving one cloud onto another

Given a `from` cloud the field becomes a map between two shapes, and `transport` can stop at any
`t`. `transport(cloudA, to = 0.5)` is a genuine intermediate distribution rather than a vertex-wise
average of two point lists.

When something upstream already knows which point goes where — a shared arc coordinate along two
curves, say — `FlowCoupling.PAIRED` uses that correspondence instead of guessing one. The target
velocity then becomes a function of `(x, t)` rather than an average over crossing paths, the loss
floor drops from the data's variance to near zero, and the result can be graded point by point: this
point was supposed to land there, and it landed here.

Doing that exposes a limit that matters when choosing the source shape. Integrating a velocity field
is a continuous invertible map, so it can deform a curve but cannot tear a loop open or join two
strands. Asking a straight segment to become a closed ring pulls the segment's two ends to the same
target point, and their paths have to cross. The left panel gives the closed target a closed source;
the right panel gives it a segment, at identical settings.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/flow_matching/topology.png" wait="2.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="520" padding="16"}

val n = 300

// Both curves are sampled in order of their own arc coordinate, so point i at one end is the same
// material point as point i at the other. That is what PAIRED needs.
fun closed(radius: Double): List<Vec3> = (0 until n).map {
    val s = it / (n - 1.0)
    vec(radius * cos(2 * PI * s), radius * sin(2 * PI * s), 0.0)
}

val target = closed(100.0)
val circleSource = closed(30.0)
val segmentSource = (0 until n).map { vec(200 * (it / (n - 1.0) - 0.5), -150.0, 0.0) }

val fromCircle = flowMatch(target, circleSource, options = options)
val fromSegment = flowMatch(target, segmentSource, options = options)

    val landed = field.transport(source, steps = 64)
    return landed.indices.sumOf { (landed[it] - target[it]).length().toDouble() } / n
}
:::fold draw the two morphs side by side and report where each point landed

    if (points.isNotEmpty()) data("m l+", points)

markdown("miss", """
    ~~~
closed source (circle -> ring)    mean landing error ${"%.2f".format(miss(fromCircle, circleSource))}
open source   (segment -> ring)   mean landing error ${"%.2f".format(miss(fromSegment, segmentSource))}

## Width along the curve

A centreline discards what the cloud says about its own spread. If the source strand is given a
constant transverse thickness and the target tube's thickness varies along its length, the field
learns both the bend and the change in width.

Here the source is a straight strand of constant width 9, and the target is a wiggling curve whose
width swells from 3 at the ends to 29 in the middle. The four panels are the source and three stages
of the flow.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/flow_matching/tube.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="560" padding="16"}

// Each sample is (s along the curve, r across it), so source and target share a point identity.
val draws: List<Pair<Double, Double>> = (0 until n).map { Pair(random(), randomGaussian()) }

fun width(s: Double): Double = 3.0 + 26.0 * sin(PI * s) * sin(PI * s)
fun centre(s: Double): Vec3 = vec(240 * (s - 0.5), 70 * sin(3 * PI * s), 0.0)

// Unit normal of the centreline: the direction the width is measured along.
fun normal(s: Double): Vec3 {
    val dy = 70.0 * 3 * PI * cos(3 * PI * s)
    val len = hypot(240.0, dy)
    return vec(-dy / len, 240.0 / len, 0.0)
}

val source = draws.map { vec(240 * (it.first - 0.5), 150 + 9 * it.second, 0.0) }
val target = draws.map { (s, r) -> centre(s) + normal(s) * (width(s) * r) }

// radius that would also contain the travel along the curve.
fun transverseSd(points: List<Vec3>, from: Double, to: Double): Double {
    val picked = draws.indices.filter { draws[it].first >= from && draws[it].first < to }
    val offsets = picked.map {
        val s = draws[it].first
        val d = points[it] - centre(s)
        (d.x * normal(s).x + d.y * normal(s).y).toDouble()
    }
    return sqrt(offsets.sumOf { it * it } / offsets.size)
}

## Settings that change the result

A few of `FlowMatchOptions`'s fields account for most of the variation, and the first two have
defaults that may surprise you.

`activation` defaults to `leaky` rather than `tanh`. A velocity field has to keep growing away from
the data — near `t = 0` the right answer is roughly `-x`, without bound — and a saturating unit
cannot, so it bends the far field back on itself. On the ring above, `tanh` gives about four times
the radial spread of `leaky` or `relu` at equal cost, more than any other setting changes it.

`finalLearningRate` decays the rate linearly across the run, and defaults to doing so. RMSProp
rescales the gradient to roughly unit length, so a constant rate keeps taking same-sized steps
however close to the answer it already is, and the fit settles at a floor set by the rate. At a
constant rate, more steps can leave the result *further* from its target; with the decay, more
steps help, and the ring's radial spread drops from 9.2 to 3.6.

`steps` is then the quality knob worth reaching for first, and the dominant cost: roughly 0.08 ms
per step at the default batch, so 6000 steps is about half a second. `hidden` defaults to two layers
of 64 units, and widening it helps much less than training longer.

`FlowMatchField.losses` records every step, so a loss still falling at the end means the run was cut
short.

## Limits of the method

The field is a deformation, so it cannot change topology: no tearing a loop, no joining two strands,
no branching. Multiple curves can be carried by one field as long as each has its own source strand
of the same kind, and they will approach each other without crossing.

`sample` returns an unordered cloud. Recovering an `FLine` from one is a separate problem, which
`transport` sidesteps by moving points you already have and keeping their order.

There is no conditioning input: one field carries one distribution onto one other. And it is a small
model — two layers of 64 units suits a few thousand points in two or three dimensions and would not
suit an image.

The API is in [Machine learning](reference/machine-learning.md); `VectorMLP` there is the
multi-output regression head that `flowMatch` trains, which is usable on its own.

`FlowMatchField.export()` takes a trained field to the GPU as an unrolled GLSL forward pass, and
`mixtureSource` builds the matched-topology source a multi-component target needs. Both are on
[Particle rules that were trained](neural_particles.md), along with what the loss on this page does
and does not tell you.

See also [Stipple transport](stipple_transport.md), which carries a uniform
sheet onto a stippled image and animates between images with one network, trained in PyTorch and
queried from Field without Python.

# Paint and pencil from FLines

`PaintCanvas` turns any [FLine](fline_examples.md) into a brushstroke of simulated oil paint, a
pencil line, hatching, a stippled area or a hand-drawn outline. The
simulation is the `paint` crate from [claude-paint](https://github.com/aliceisjustplaying/claude-paint),
by alice ([@aliceisjustplaying](https://github.com/aliceisjustplaying)), MIT licensed. It models
a brush as individual bristles that carry paint and run out. Paint mixes on the canvas like pigment,
so blue into yellow makes green. Each stroke stays wet, stiffening and drying over simulated minutes.
The same canvas can be a sheet of paper for [watercolour and ink](watercolor.md), and its
brushes can have [hairs that move](paint_gestures.md).
Field calls it through a small native library, which you build once (see
[Building the library](#building-the-library)). The examples below are also in the
[paint_canvas](agent_transcripts.md#paint_canvas) starting point, and the classes they use
(`PaintCanvas`, `PaintBrush`, `Pencil`, `Tubes`, in `afield.graphics.paint`) each have their own KDoc.

Here is a canvas, a brush and three strokes. The brush is loaded before the first stroke and again
before the second. The third stroke is a zigzag with no reload, so the brush runs dry along it.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/paint_canvas/first.png" alt="a white canvas with three horizontal brushstrokes. The top one is a wavy band of deep blue with soft bristle-streaked edges. The middle one is the same shape in orange-yellow. The bottom is a zigzag of three passes in a lighter yellow: the first pass is solid, and the later passes thin out and break up towards their ends as the brush runs out of paint" wait="10" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20" requires="paint" name="first" embed=true}

import afield.graphics.paint.*

val canvas = PaintCanvas(900, aspect = 1.6)
val brush = canvas.brush(BrushKind.Filbert, width = 45.0)

brush.load(rgb(0.15, 0.3, 0.65))
canvas.stroke(FLine().moveTo(80, 140).cubicTo(330, 40, 630, 240, 920, 120), brush)

brush.load(rgb(0.95, 0.7, 0.15))
canvas.stroke(FLine().moveTo(80, 330).cubicTo(330, 230, 630, 430, 920, 310), brush)

// no reload: three more passes, and the brush runs out along the way
val zigzag = FLine().moveTo(80, 470)
for (i in 1..3) zigzag.lineTo(if (i % 2 == 1) 920 else 80, 470 + i * 40)
canvas.stroke(zigzag, brush)

display("main", canvas.png())
```

A few things in that box apply everywhere on this page:

- **Coordinates.** The canvas is always 1000 units wide and `1000 / aspect` units tall, with y
  growing downwards, whatever its pixel width. `PaintCanvas(900, aspect = 1.6)` is 900 by 563
  pixels and 1000 by 625 units. To paint lines you drew somewhere else, pass `view = Rect(...)`: that
  rectangle of FLine coordinates is stretched over the whole canvas.
- **One stroke per subpath.** Each `moveTo` starts a new movement of the hand. The brush is not
  reloaded between subpaths, so a line with many pieces uses up its paint the way a real brush would.
- **Colours** are `rgb(...)` values, the same sRGB colours as everywhere else in Field.
- **`png()`** renders the canvas and encodes it, and `display` shows the bytes as an image. Its
  `relief` argument (0.6 by default) lights the thickness of the paint from the upper left, which is
  what makes the bristle ridges visible.

`BrushKind` has six brushes. Below, each one draws the same curve, loaded with the same dark paint.
From left to right: `Round`, `HogFlat`, `Filbert`, `Fan`, `Rigger` and `Badger`.

import afield.graphics.paint.*

val canvas = PaintCanvas(900, aspect = 2.0)
BrushKind.entries.forEachIndexed { i, kind ->
    val x = 110.0 + i * 155
    val brush = canvas.brush(kind, width = 40.0).load(rgb(0.12, 0.12, 0.18))
    canvas.stroke(FLine().moveTo(x, 70).cubicTo(x + 60, 200, x - 60, 300, x, 430), brush)

`width` is the brush's width at full pressure, in canvas units. A brush gets wider when pressed
harder, so `stroke(..., pressure = 0.3..0.9)` gives a stroke that starts thin and swells.
`point = 1.0` gives a round or rigger brush a fine tip. Pressed lightly, only the tip touches, and
the mark draws down to a point as the brush lifts.

## Paint, and paint over paint

`load` takes the paint's colour and three properties that change how strokes look:

- `hiding`: how much one coat covers what is underneath. About 0.05 is a transparent glaze, 0.5 a
  scumble, and the default 0.92 is opaque body colour.
- `stiff`: 0 is fluid paint that levels out as it dries. 1 is stiff paint straight from the tube,
  which keeps its brush marks.
- `wipe`: how much of the paint already in the brush is wiped off first. The default is 0.85, so a
  little of the previous colour always comes along. Use `wipe = 1.0` for a clean brush, or something
  like 0.4 to blend each colour into the last.

On the left below, a dark band is dried and then crossed by white at hiding 0.05, 0.5 and 0.92. On
the right, a blue stroke crosses a yellow one twice. At the top the yellow is still wet, and the blue
drags through it and mixes into green. At the bottom the yellow was dried first with `dry()`, so the
blue sits on top of it.

Where the upper blue crosses the wet yellow it turns streaky green, with blue and yellow pulled through each other along the bristle lines. val light = canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width = 70.0)

canvas.stroke(FLine().moveTo(750, 60).lineTo(750, 220), blue.load(rgb(0.1, 0.25, 0.7)), shake = 0.3)
canvas.stroke(FLine().moveTo(540, 360).lineTo(960, 360), yellow.load(rgb(0.95, 0.8, 0.1)), shake = 0.3)

`wait(minutes)` lets simulated time pass without drying everything. Paint keeps stiffening for as
long as you wait, and how fast depends on its thickness and its `drying` rate. `dry()` waits until
every stroke is touch-dry. Neither rendering nor `png()` changes the canvas: they show a dried copy,
and the strokes you have laid stay wet for the next one.

## Strokes from any FLine

A stroke can come from anything that makes an FLine. This box follows a flow field. Each stroke
starts at a random point and takes 30 short steps in the field's direction. Before each stroke the
brush is reloaded with a colour that depends on where the stroke ends, using `wipe = 0.4`, so every
stroke carries some of the last one's colour and neighbouring strokes blend.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/paint_canvas/flow.png" alt="a white canvas filled with a few hundred short, curved, thick brushstrokes that sweep together in swirling feather-like currents. Colours drift from warm yellow, orange and magenta at the top to violet, teal and blue at the bottom, and neighbouring strokes share and blend colours where they overlap. Relief lighting shows bristle ridges and the raised edges of each stroke" wait="20" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20" requires="paint" name="flow" embed=true}
:::static
import afield.graphics.paint.*
import kotlin.random.Random

val canvas = PaintCanvas(900, aspect = 1.4, seed = 4)
val brush = canvas.brush(BrushKind.Filbert, width = 16.0)
val rnd = Random(4)

// the direction of the field at (x, y)
fun angle(x: Double, y: Double) = sin(x * 0.006) * 2.0 + cos(y * 0.008 + x * 0.002) * 1.5

repeat(260) {
    var x = rnd.nextDouble(0.0, 1000.0)
    var y = rnd.nextDouble(0.0, canvas.heightUnits)
    val line = FLine().moveTo(x, y)
    repeat(30) {
        val a = angle(x, y)
        x += cos(a) * 6
        y += sin(a) * 6
        line.lineTo(x, y)
    }
    val t = y / canvas.heightUnits
    brush.load(rgb(0.9 - 0.6 * t, 0.4 + 0.3 * sin(x * 0.01), 0.2 + 0.6 * t), stiff = 0.9, wipe = 0.4)
    canvas.stroke(line, brush, pressure = 0.5..0.9)
}
display("main", canvas.png(relief = 0.8))
```

## Pencil and chalk

The same canvas takes graphite and chalk. `canvas.pencil("2B")` is a pencil of that grade, from
`"9H"` to `"9B"`, and `canvas.chalk()` is a stick of black chalk. There are three ways to draw with
them:

- `draw(line, pencil, pressure)` draws each subpath as one line, smoothed and wavering slightly.
  Pass `ruler = true` for a straight, ruled line.
- `sketch(line, pencil, passes = 3)` makes several light, broken passes along a line, each
  wandering a little off it.
- `hatch(region, pencil, angle, spacing)` fills a closed FLine with short parallel strokes.

A pencil wears as it draws, so its line widens; `pencil.sharpen()` starts it fresh.

Every mark has a real physical size: a pencil point is about 0.3 mm. On the default 700 mm canvas
that is a fifth of a pixel at 900 pixels wide, so for drawing, give the canvas a smaller sheet with
`sizeMm`. This one is 20 cm wide.

The vase's two sides are sketched in thin light grey lines that break off in places and leave its top open. Its right side is hatched with close diagonal strokes of a softer, darker pencil that crowd together towards the bottom. A straight ruled line of grainy black chalk runs across the full width for the table edge" wait="10" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20" requires="paint" name="drawing" embed=true}
:::static

val canvas = PaintCanvas(900, aspect = 1.5, sizeMm = 200.0)

val vase = FLine().moveTo(420, 120).cubicTo(330, 220, 300, 420, 380, 560)
    .lineTo(620, 560).cubicTo(700, 420, 670, 220, 580, 120)
canvas.sketch(vase, canvas.pencil("2B"), pressure = 0.5, passes = 3)

// hatch the shadow side with a softer pencil
val shadow = FLine().moveTo(560, 140).cubicTo(650, 240, 680, 420, 610, 550).lineTo(540, 550)
    .cubicTo(600, 420, 590, 240, 520, 140).lineTo(560, 140)
canvas.hatch(shadow, canvas.pencil("4B"), angle = 1.0, spacing = 7.0, length = 50.0)

// the table edge, ruled in chalk
canvas.draw(FLine().moveTo(80, 560).lineTo(920, 560), canvas.chalk(), pressure = 0.7, ruler = true)

display("main", canvas.png(relief = 0.0))
```

Graphite stays loose until something seals it. `erase(region, strength)` lifts it the way a
kneaded eraser does: more from the tops of the paper's grain than from the hollows, and never quite
all of it. `fixDrawing()` sprays fixative, after which the eraser no longer lifts it. Paint laid over
graphite seals it into the picture, and graphite does not take on wet paint.

## Areas: worked, stippled, outlined

Three methods fill or bound a whole area at once. Each one takes a *region*: a closed FLine, where
a ring inside another ring makes a hole.

- `work(region, color, handling)` paints the region with many strokes, planned the way the
  crate's painters block in an area: stroke length and direction, curvature, broken and restated
  strokes, and trips back to the palette. `Handling` picks the kind of strokes: `Broad`, `Body`,
  `Detail`, `Hatch`, `Glaze`, `Scumble`, or `Blend`, a clean blender that only softens wet paint
  already there. You can override the angle, length, coverage and brush width.
- `stipple(region, color, size, coverage)` covers the region with separate touches of an upright
  brush. `feather` thins them out towards the edge.
- `outline(line, brush, character)` turns a few rough points into the line a hand would draw: it
  lifts and starts again, overshoots corners and restates stretches. The character is `Firm`,
  `Searching`, `Broken` or `Soft`. It returns the strokes as an FLine, so you can draw them
  elsewhere too, and with `brush = null` it paints nothing and only returns them.

From left to right below: a region worked in blue `Body` strokes, then its top half worked again
with `Broad` strokes of a pale colour while the blue is still wet; a feathered stipple; and a
triangle from four rough points, drawn by a `Searching` hand.

For single marks there is `touch(brush, x, y)`, which presses the brush tip down and lifts it with
no path: a dab. `drag`, `twist` and `angle` move, roll and turn the tip while it is down.

## A drawing under the paint

Pencil and paint share one canvas, so the usual order of work holds: draw first, then paint over
the drawing. Graphite under thin paint shows through, and wherever paint goes over it, it is sealed
into the picture. That gives `hiding` a second job: it decides how much of the drawing survives.

Here a landscape is sketched in 3B, then painted with `work`. The sky is a `Glaze` at hiding
0.25 and the grass is `Broad` strokes at 0.35, so the hill line and the tree trunk read through
both. The tree's crown is `Body` strokes at 0.6, which mostly cover its drawing.

## Tube paints, glazes and age

Instead of a colour, a brush can be loaded from the crate's catalogue of historical tube paints,
mixed by parts: `brush.load(mapOf("lead white" to 3.0, "vermilion" to 1.0))`. The tubes mix the way
paint does, weighted by how strongly each pigment tints, and the pile keeps their hiding, stiffness
and drying rate. `Tubes.names` lists the catalogue, `Tubes["smalt"]` describes one tube,
`Tubes.mix(...)` gives the colour of a mixture without painting it, and `Tubes.mixSpectral(...)`
mixes any colours as pigments rather than as light.

Two more steps finish a painting:

- `glaze(color, region, coats)` lays a transparent film over dry paint. Over the whole canvas,
  a thin warm glaze looks like old varnish.
- `crack()` grows craquelure through the paint and ground, with cupping and dirt in the cracks.
  `CrackKind.Aged` gives a hierarchy of cracks that developed unevenly, and `CrackKind.Even` one
  uniform network. Cracks open a few dozen micrometres, so like pencil they need a small `sizeMm`
  to show.

This one mixes each band from two parts lead white to one part of a different tube, dries the
painting, glazes it lightly and cracks it.

## Knives, rags and spatter

Three more tools work the paint without a brush:

- `canvas.knife(width)` is a painting knife, and `knife.load(color)` puts a bead of paint on its
  blade. `canvas.knife(line, knife)` pulls it along a line. The flexible blade rests on the high
  points of the surface and lays a flat-topped slab below its edge, pressing paint out into ridges
  at its ends and leaving a bead where it lifts. `canvas.scrape(line, knife)` presses hard and lays
  nothing: it cuts the wet paint off down to the dry surface, and the blade keeps what it cut.
- `canvas.rag(width)` is a cotton rag bunched into a pad. `canvas.wipe(line, rag)` lifts open paint
  along a line in streaks, where the creases of the cloth touch, and `canvas.blot(rag, x, y)` presses
  it down once. Paint that has begun to set no longer comes away. The face of the rag loads up as it
  works; `canvas.refold(rag)` turns a cleaner face out and `canvas.dampen(rag)` wets it with spirits,
  so that it lifts nearly to the ground.
- `canvas.spatter(brush, x, y, toward)` flicks a loaded brush. Only the paint the hairs can't hold
  flies off, so fluid paint spatters and stiff paint barely does: load with `turps` (turpentine,
  0..0.9 of the paint's volume) for a wet flick. Each drop comes off one hair, so a brush loaded with
  two colours, one on each side (`part = LoadPart(side = ...)`), spatters both.

All three report what they move. `wipe` and `blot` return the mm³ of paint they lifted,
`canvas.carried(knife)` is the paint on the blade, and `stats.wetPaintMm3` is the wet paint left on
the canvas; a scrape takes off the canvas exactly what it puts on the blade.

The box below lays a dark passage, wipes two lights out of it with a rag, knifes a pale band across
it and scrapes through that, then spatters a double-loaded brush. A low lamp from the upper left
(`light = PaintLight.Raking`) shows the slab's ridges and the shine of the wet paint.

## Brushes made to order

A `BrushKind` is a starting point. `brush(kind, width, config = BrushConfig(...))` changes how the
brush is made: `bristles` (how many hairs it is simulated with), `stiffness` (0 soft sable to 1
stiff hog), `length` (how far the tips trail behind the contact), `lay` (how thick a full brush
lays paint), `run` (how far a load lasts), `pickup` and `push` (how much wet paint each hair takes
up or ploughs aside), `splay`, `ragged` and `point`. Anything left out keeps the kind's own value,
and `brush.config` reads back what the brush is. Below, the same hog flat, each dipped in the same
paint and stroked the same way: as it comes, with 12 bristles, with 40 ragged ones, taking up and
ploughing aside most of the paint it passes over, and laying a thin film that lasts:

## Brushes that stay dirty

A brush keeps what it picks up. Stroked through wet paint, it carries some of that colour into its
next stroke, and `load` mixes new paint into what is left unless `wipe` takes it out first. To come
back to the same brush later, keep it: a `PaintToolbox` holds brushes, knives, rags and pencils by
name.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val tools = PaintToolbox()
tools["sky"] = canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, 45.0)
tools.brush("sky").load(rgb(0.45, 0.55, 0.75))
canvas.stroke(sky, tools.brush("sky"))
// later, dirty with the earth it was dragged through
canvas.stroke(horizon, tools.brush("sky"))
tools.save(file)                      // every bristle's paint, the knife's bead, the rag's faces
val again = PaintToolbox.load(file)   // carries on exactly as the tools would have
```

`canvas.carried(brush)` reports the colour and volume of the paint in a brush, and
`tools.describe(canvas)` says the same for every tool. Each tool also snapshots on its own:
`brush.state()` and `PaintBrush.restore(state)`. [AI4 paints](ai4_painting.md) keeps its painter's
brushes this way, so a conversation rewound to an earlier request gets its brushes back as dirty as
they were.

## The canvas itself

`PaintCanvas(widthPx, aspect, ground, groundColor, seed, view, sizeMm, engine)`:

- `ground` is what the canvas starts as:
    - `PaintGround.Bare`, the default, is a flat ground of `groundColor` (white by default).
    - `PaintGround.Oil` is the crate's prepared oil canvas: woven linen, sized and primed with a
      warm red-brown ground. Its texture shows through thin paint and catches the relief lighting.
    - `PaintGround.OilRedGround` is a red-brown layer under two pale knifed and rolled grounds.
    - `PaintGround.Linen` is raw linen in `groundColor`, for priming yourself with
      `prime(color, microns = ...)`. `prime(..., absorbent = 1.0)` makes that ground a chalk and
      glue one, which draws oil out of the paint laid on it, so the paint dries leaner and matte.
    - `PaintGround.RawCotton` and `PaintGround.RawLinen` are bare cloth in its own colour, with no
      ground at all, as soak-stain painters used it.

    `groundColor` only applies to `Bare` and `Linen`.
- `sizeMm` is the canvas's physical width. It changes nothing about the coordinates, only how big
  the real-sized things in the simulation look: bristles, pencil points, the linen weave, cracks.
- `seed` seeds every brush, pencil mark and crack, and the linen of an oil ground. The same seed and
  the same calls always paint the same picture.
- `engine` is the version of the simulation to paint with, the newest by default
  (`PaintCanvas.engine`). An engine never changes, so the same calls on the same engine always
  paint the same pixels, and a saved canvas opens with the engine it was painted with. Thinned
  paint and raw cloth need engine 3 or later; stiff impasto, clumping hair, turpentine, absorbent
  grounds and matte or glossy surfaces need engine 4; the knife's torn edges need engine 5. Oil
  paint dries 2.5 times more slowly from engine 3 on.

Looking at it, and keeping it:

- `png()` and `render()` show a dried copy, the way the painting will look. `render(wet = true)`
  shows it as it looks right now, wet paint and all. `light = PaintLight(azimuth, elevation)` looks
  at it under a lamp instead of the default relief lighting: ridges cast shadows along the light,
  and wet paint shines. `PaintLight.Raking` is a low lamp from the upper left, `PaintLight.Gallery`
  a high one.
- `stats` reports the simulated clock, an estimate of the hand time the marks would take a painter,
  how much of the canvas is still open, setting, tacky or dry, and the wet paint and solvent on it
  in mm³.
- `copy()` is an independent copy, wet paint included, for trying something out.
  `saveState(path)` writes the whole canvas to a file and `PaintCanvas.load(path)` carries on from
  it. `save(path)` writes a PNG.

A canvas and its brushes hold native memory. It is freed when they are garbage-collected, or straight
away with `close()` (both are `AutoCloseable`, so `use { }` works).

`rustc`); older distribution packages may be too old for this crate. `--setup` checks their

# Paint and pencil from FLines

`PaintCanvas` turns any [FLine](fline_examples.md) into a brushstroke of simulated oil paint, a
pencil line, hatching, a stippled area or a hand-drawn outline. The
simulation is the `paint` crate from [claude-paint](https://github.com/aliceisjustplaying/claude-paint),
by alice ([@aliceisjustplaying](https://github.com/aliceisjustplaying)), MIT licensed. It models
a brush as individual bristles that carry paint and run out. Paint mixes on the canvas like pigment,
so blue into yellow makes green. Each stroke stays wet, stiffening and drying over simulated minutes.
The same canvas can be a sheet of paper for [watercolour and ink](watercolor.md), and its
brushes can have [hairs that move](paint_gestures.md).
Field calls it through a small native library, which you build once (see
[Building the library](#building-the-library)). The examples below are also in the
[paint_canvas](agent_transcripts.md#paint_canvas) starting point, and the classes they use
(`PaintCanvas`, `PaintBrush`, `Pencil`, `Tubes`, in `afield.graphics.paint`) each have their own KDoc.

Here is a canvas, a brush and three strokes. The brush is loaded before the first stroke and again
before the second. The third stroke is a zigzag with no reload, so the brush runs dry along it.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/paint_canvas/first.png" alt="a white canvas with three horizontal brushstrokes. The top one is a wavy band of deep blue with soft bristle-streaked edges. The middle one is the same shape in orange-yellow. The bottom is a zigzag of three passes in a lighter yellow: the first pass is solid, and the later passes thin out and break up towards their ends as the brush runs out of paint" wait="10" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20" requires="paint" name="first" embed=true}
:::static
import afield.graphics.paint.*

val canvas = PaintCanvas(900, aspect = 1.6)
val brush = canvas.brush(BrushKind.Filbert, width = 45.0)

brush.load(rgb(0.15, 0.3, 0.65))
canvas.stroke(FLine().moveTo(80, 140).cubicTo(330, 40, 630, 240, 920, 120), brush)

brush.load(rgb(0.95, 0.7, 0.15))
canvas.stroke(FLine().moveTo(80, 330).cubicTo(330, 230, 630, 430, 920, 310), brush)

// no reload: three more passes, and the brush runs out along the way
val zigzag = FLine().moveTo(80, 470)
for (i in 1..3) zigzag.lineTo(if (i % 2 == 1) 920 else 80, 470 + i * 40)
canvas.stroke(zigzag, brush)

display("main", canvas.png())
```

A few things in that box apply everywhere on this page:

- **Coordinates.** The canvas is always 1000 units wide and `1000 / aspect` units tall, with y
  growing downwards, whatever its pixel width. `PaintCanvas(900, aspect = 1.6)` is 900 by 563
  pixels and 1000 by 625 units. To paint lines you drew somewhere else, pass `view = Rect(...)`: that
  rectangle of FLine coordinates is stretched over the whole canvas.
- **One stroke per subpath.** Each `moveTo` starts a new movement of the hand. The brush is not
  reloaded between subpaths, so a line with many pieces uses up its paint the way a real brush would.
- **Colours** are `rgb(...)` values, the same sRGB colours as everywhere else in Field.
- **`png()`** renders the canvas and encodes it, and `display` shows the bytes as an image. Its
  `relief` argument (0.6 by default) lights the thickness of the paint from the upper left, which is
  what makes the bristle ridges visible.

`BrushKind` has six brushes. Below, each one draws the same curve, loaded with the same dark paint.
From left to right: `Round`, `HogFlat`, `Filbert`, `Fan`, `Rigger` and `Badger`.

`width` is the brush's width at full pressure, in canvas units. A brush gets wider when pressed

the mark draws down to a point as the brush lifts.

## Paint, and paint over paint

`load` takes the paint's colour and three properties that change how strokes look:

- `hiding`: how much one coat covers what is underneath. About 0.05 is a transparent glaze, 0.5 a
  scumble, and the default 0.92 is opaque body colour.
- `stiff`: 0 is fluid paint that levels out as it dries. 1 is stiff paint straight from the tube,
  which keeps its brush marks.
- `wipe`: how much of the paint already in the brush is wiped off first. The default is 0.85, so a
  little of the previous colour always comes along. Use `wipe = 1.0` for a clean brush, or something
  like 0.4 to blend each colour into the last.

On the left below, a dark band is dried and then crossed by white at hiding 0.05, 0.5 and 0.92. On
the right, a blue stroke crosses a yellow one twice. At the top the yellow is still wet, and the blue
drags through it and mixes into green. At the bottom the yellow was dried first with `dry()`, so the
blue sits on top of it.

long as you wait, and how fast depends on its thickness and its `drying` rate. `dry()` waits until

and the strokes you have laid stay wet for the next one.

## Strokes from any FLine

A stroke can come from anything that makes an FLine. This box follows a flow field. Each stroke
starts at a random point and takes 30 short steps in the field's direction. Before each stroke the
brush is reloaded with a colour that depends on where the stroke ends, using `wipe = 0.4`, so every
stroke carries some of the last one's colour and neighbouring strokes blend.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/paint_canvas/flow.png" alt="a white canvas filled with a few hundred short, curved, thick brushstrokes that sweep together in swirling feather-like currents. Colours drift from warm yellow, orange and magenta at the top to violet, teal and blue at the bottom, and neighbouring strokes share and blend colours where they overlap. Relief lighting shows bristle ridges and the raised edges of each stroke" wait="20" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20" requires="paint" name="flow" embed=true}

import afield.graphics.paint.*
import kotlin.random.Random

val canvas = PaintCanvas(900, aspect = 1.4, seed = 4)
val brush = canvas.brush(BrushKind.Filbert, width = 16.0)
val rnd = Random(4)

// the direction of the field at (x, y)
fun angle(x: Double, y: Double) = sin(x * 0.006) * 2.0 + cos(y * 0.008 + x * 0.002) * 1.5

repeat(260) {
    var x = rnd.nextDouble(0.0, 1000.0)
    var y = rnd.nextDouble(0.0, canvas.heightUnits)
    val line = FLine().moveTo(x, y)
    repeat(30) {
        val a = angle(x, y)
        x += cos(a) * 6
        y += sin(a) * 6
        line.lineTo(x, y)
    }
    val t = y / canvas.heightUnits
    brush.load(rgb(0.9 - 0.6 * t, 0.4 + 0.3 * sin(x * 0.01), 0.2 + 0.6 * t), stiff = 0.9, wipe = 0.4)
    canvas.stroke(line, brush, pressure = 0.5..0.9)
}
display("main", canvas.png(relief = 0.8))
```

## Pencil and chalk

The same canvas takes graphite and chalk. `canvas.pencil("2B")` is a pencil of that grade, from
`"9H"` to `"9B"`, and `canvas.chalk()` is a stick of black chalk. There are three ways to draw with
them:

- `draw(line, pencil, pressure)` draws each subpath as one line, smoothed and wavering slightly.
  Pass `ruler = true` for a straight, ruled line.
- `sketch(line, pencil, passes = 3)` makes several light, broken passes along a line, each
  wandering a little off it.
- `hatch(region, pencil, angle, spacing)` fills a closed FLine with short parallel strokes.

A pencil wears as it draws, so its line widens; `pencil.sharpen()` starts it fresh.

Every mark has a real physical size: a pencil point is about 0.3 mm. On the default 700 mm canvas
that is a fifth of a pixel at 900 pixels wide, so for drawing, give the canvas a smaller sheet with
`sizeMm`. This one is 20 cm wide.

Graphite stays loose until something seals it. `erase(region, strength)` lifts it the way a
kneaded eraser does: more from the tops of the paper's grain than from the hollows, and never quite
all of it. `fixDrawing()` sprays fixative, after which the eraser no longer lifts it. Paint laid over
graphite seals it into the picture, and graphite does not take on wet paint.

## Areas: worked, stippled, outlined

Three methods fill or bound a whole area at once. Each one takes a *region*: a closed FLine, where
a ring inside another ring makes a hole.

- `work(region, color, handling)` paints the region with many strokes, planned the way the
  crate's painters block in an area: stroke length and direction, curvature, broken and restated
  strokes, and trips back to the palette. `Handling` picks the kind of strokes: `Broad`, `Body`,
  `Detail`, `Hatch`, `Glaze`, `Scumble`, or `Blend`, a clean blender that only softens wet paint
  already there. You can override the angle, length, coverage and brush width.
- `stipple(region, color, size, coverage)` covers the region with separate touches of an upright
  brush. `feather` thins them out towards the edge.
- `outline(line, brush, character)` turns a few rough points into the line a hand would draw: it
  lifts and starts again, overshoots corners and restates stretches. The character is `Firm`,
  `Searching`, `Broken` or `Soft`. It returns the strokes as an FLine, so you can draw them
  elsewhere too, and with `brush = null` it paints nothing and only returns them.

From left to right below: a region worked in blue `Body` strokes, then its top half worked again
with `Broad` strokes of a pale colour while the blue is still wet; a feathered stipple; and a
triangle from four rough points, drawn by a `Searching` hand.

## Tube paints, glazes and age

Instead of a colour, a brush can be loaded from the crate's catalogue of historical tube paints,
mixed by parts: `brush.load(mapOf("lead white" to 3.0, "vermilion" to 1.0))`. The tubes mix the way
paint does, weighted by how strongly each pigment tints, and the pile keeps their hiding, stiffness
and drying rate. `Tubes.names` lists the catalogue, `Tubes["smalt"]` describes one tube,
`Tubes.mix(...)` gives the colour of a mixture without painting it, and `Tubes.mixSpectral(...)`
mixes any colours as pigments rather than as light.

Two more steps finish a painting:

- `glaze(color, region, coats)` lays a transparent film over dry paint. Over the whole canvas,
  a thin warm glaze looks like old varnish.
- `crack()` grows craquelure through the paint and ground, with cupping and dirt in the cracks.
  `CrackKind.Aged` gives a hierarchy of cracks that developed unevenly, and `CrackKind.Even` one
  uniform network. Cracks open a few dozen micrometres, so like pencil they need a small `sizeMm`
  to show.

This one mixes each band from two parts lead white to one part of a different tube, dries the
painting, glazes it lightly and cracks it.

## Knives, rags and spatter

Three more tools work the paint without a brush:

- `canvas.knife(width)` is a painting knife, and `knife.load(color)` puts a bead of paint on its
  blade. `canvas.knife(line, knife)` pulls it along a line. The flexible blade rests on the high
  points of the surface and lays a flat-topped slab below its edge, pressing paint out into ridges
  at its ends and leaving a bead where it lifts. `canvas.scrape(line, knife)` presses hard and lays
  nothing: it cuts the wet paint off down to the dry surface, and the blade keeps what it cut.
- `canvas.rag(width)` is a cotton rag bunched into a pad. `canvas.wipe(line, rag)` lifts open paint
  along a line in streaks, where the creases of the cloth touch, and `canvas.blot(rag, x, y)` presses
  it down once. Paint that has begun to set no longer comes away. The face of the rag loads up as it
  works; `canvas.refold(rag)` turns a cleaner face out and `canvas.dampen(rag)` wets it with spirits,
  so that it lifts nearly to the ground.
- `canvas.spatter(brush, x, y, toward)` flicks a loaded brush. Only the paint the hairs can't hold
  flies off, so fluid paint spatters and stiff paint barely does: load with `turps` (turpentine,
  0..0.9 of the paint's volume) for a wet flick. Each drop comes off one hair, so a brush loaded with
  two colours, one on each side (`part = LoadPart(side = ...)`), spatters both.

All three report what they move. `wipe` and `blot` return the mm³ of paint they lifted,
`canvas.carried(knife)` is the paint on the blade, and `stats.wetPaintMm3` is the wet paint left on
the canvas; a scrape takes off the canvas exactly what it puts on the blade.

The box below lays a dark passage, wipes two lights out of it with a rag, knifes a pale band across
it and scrapes through that, then spatters a double-loaded brush. A low lamp from the upper left
(`light = PaintLight.Raking`) shows the slab's ridges and the shine of the wet paint.

A `BrushKind` is a starting point. `brush(kind, width, config = BrushConfig(...))` changes how the
brush is made: `bristles` (how many hairs it is simulated with), `stiffness` (0 soft sable to 1
stiff hog), `length` (how far the tips trail behind the contact), `lay` (how thick a full brush
lays paint), `run` (how far a load lasts), `pickup` and `push` (how much wet paint each hair takes
up or ploughs aside), `splay`, `ragged` and `point`. Anything left out keeps the kind's own value,
and `brush.config` reads back what the brush is. Below, the same hog flat, each dipped in the same
paint and stroked the same way: as it comes, with 12 bristles, with 40 ragged ones, taking up and
ploughing aside most of the paint it passes over, and laying a thin film that lasts:

## Brushes that stay dirty

A brush keeps what it picks up. Stroked through wet paint, it carries some of that colour into its
next stroke, and `load` mixes new paint into what is left unless `wipe` takes it out first. To come
back to the same brush later, keep it: a `PaintToolbox` holds brushes, knives, rags and pencils by
name.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val tools = PaintToolbox()
tools["sky"] = canvas.brush(BrushKind.HogFlat, 45.0)
tools.brush("sky").load(rgb(0.45, 0.55, 0.75))
canvas.stroke(sky, tools.brush("sky"))
// later, dirty with the earth it was dragged through
canvas.stroke(horizon, tools.brush("sky"))
tools.save(file)                      // every bristle's paint, the knife's bead, the rag's faces
val again = PaintToolbox.load(file)   // carries on exactly as the tools would have
```

`canvas.carried(brush)` reports the colour and volume of the paint in a brush, and
`tools.describe(canvas)` says the same for every tool. Each tool also snapshots on its own:
`brush.state()` and `PaintBrush.restore(state)`. [AI4 paints](ai4_painting.md) keeps its painter's
brushes this way, so a conversation rewound to an earlier request gets its brushes back as dirty as
they were.

## The canvas itself

`PaintCanvas(widthPx, aspect, ground, groundColor, seed, view, sizeMm, engine)`:

- `ground` is what the canvas starts as:
    - `PaintGround.Bare`, the default, is a flat ground of `groundColor` (white by default).
    - `PaintGround.Oil` is the crate's prepared oil canvas: woven linen, sized and primed with a
      warm red-brown ground. Its texture shows through thin paint and catches the relief lighting.
    - `PaintGround.OilRedGround` is a red-brown layer under two pale knifed and rolled grounds.
    - `PaintGround.Linen` is raw linen in `groundColor`, for priming yourself with
      `prime(color, microns = ...)`. `prime(..., absorbent = 1.0)` makes that ground a chalk and
      glue one, which draws oil out of the paint laid on it, so the paint dries leaner and matte.
    - `PaintGround.RawCotton` and `PaintGround.RawLinen` are bare cloth in its own colour, with no
      ground at all, as soak-stain painters used it.

    `groundColor` only applies to `Bare` and `Linen`.
- `sizeMm` is the canvas's physical width. It changes nothing about the coordinates, only how big
  the real-sized things in the simulation look: bristles, pencil points, the linen weave, cracks.
- `seed` seeds every brush, pencil mark and crack, and the linen of an oil ground. The same seed and
  the same calls always paint the same picture.
- `engine` is the version of the simulation to paint with, the newest by default
  (`PaintCanvas.engine`). An engine never changes, so the same calls on the same engine always
  paint the same pixels, and a saved canvas opens with the engine it was painted with. Thinned
  paint and raw cloth need engine 3 or later; stiff impasto, clumping hair, turpentine, absorbent
  grounds and matte or glossy surfaces need engine 4; the knife's torn edges need engine 5. Oil
  paint dries 2.5 times more slowly from engine 3 on.

Looking at it, and keeping it:

- `png()` and `render()` show a dried copy, the way the painting will look. `render(wet = true)`
  shows it as it looks right now, wet paint and all. `light = PaintLight(azimuth, elevation)` looks
  at it under a lamp instead of the default relief lighting: ridges cast shadows along the light,
  and wet paint shines. `PaintLight.Raking` is a low lamp from the upper left, `PaintLight.Gallery`
  a high one.
- `stats` reports the simulated clock, an estimate of the hand time the marks would take a painter,
  how much of the canvas is still open, setting, tacky or dry, and the wet paint and solvent on it
  in mm³.
- `copy()` is an independent copy, wet paint included, for trying something out.
  `saveState(path)` writes the whole canvas to a file and `PaintCanvas.load(path)` carries on from
  it. `save(path)` writes a PNG.

A canvas and its brushes hold native memory. It is freed when they are garbage-collected, or straight
away with `close()` (both are `AutoCloseable`, so `use { }` works).

## Building the library

The simulation is Rust. Field calls it through a small wrapper library in [native/field-paint](https://github.com/OpenEndedGroup/Field4/blob/main/native/field-paint),
which is not part of the normal build. Install a current stable Rust toolchain (`cargo` and
`rustc`); older distribution packages may be too old for this crate. `--setup` checks their
versions before preparing paint. Build it once:

```diffstatic {data-lang=bash}
./gradlew buildPaintNative
```

The crate is alice's [claude-paint](https://github.com/aliceisjustplaying/claude-paint) `paint`
crate, kept in the repository at [native/field-paint/vendor/paint](https://github.com/OpenEndedGroup/Field4/blob/main/native/field-paint/vendor/paint) under its MIT licence, with the
upstream commit it was taken from in [VENDORED.md](https://github.com/OpenEndedGroup/Field4/blob/main/native/field-paint/vendor/paint/VENDORED.md). Field's additions to it are in its

# Brushes with moving hairs

An ordinary [PaintCanvas](paint_canvas.md) brush places its bristles by rule: they follow the
path, and the tips trail a little behind. `canvas.dynamicBrush(...)` makes a brush whose hairs are
simulated instead. Each hair is a chain of short segments that bends, drags on the surface, sticks
and slides, splays when it is pressed and springs back when it is lifted. Where the hairs touch,
they lay and pick up paint, oil or watercolour. A brush pressed hard and dragged sideways for long
enough keeps a set, as a real one does.

Because the hairs have mass and stiffness, it matters how the hand moves, not only where. A
`TimedGesture` gives the brush's position over time, how hard it presses, and how the handle is
tilted and turned. The same path drawn slowly, fast, with a pause, tilted or rolled gives different
marks.

Here is a round brush drawn along the same curve at 20, 80 and 300 mm/s, and then right to left.
The slow stroke lays the most paint and runs out first; the fast one lays thinner paint and carries
it further.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/paint_gestures/speed.png" alt="four wavy horizontal brushstrokes of dark brown on cream paper. The fourth goes right to left, dark and blunt at its right-hand start and fading to the left" wait="20" timeout="600" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20" requires="paint" name="speed" embed=true}

[`BrushConfig`](paint_canvas.md#brushes-made-to-order) as an ordinary brush, with the number of
hairs to simulate (32 by default) and the segments in each (5). It loads like one, `load(color,

FLine. Every stroke is simulated in 1 ms steps, so a long slow stroke takes longer to paint than
with an ordinary brush.

## Gestures

`canvas.gesture(line, speed, pressure, tilt, lean, roll)` turns an FLine into a `TimedGesture`:

- `speed` is in mm/s along the path, so the time a stroke takes depends on the canvas's `sizeMm`.
- `pressure` is one value, a start and an end, or a profile at evenly spaced points along each
  subpath. At 0 the tips just touch, at 1 the ferrule is pressed down by 60% of the hairs' length,
  and more presses harder still. Below 0 the brush is lifted clear of the surface, so a stroke that
  ends below 0 leaves the paper.
- `tilt` is the handle's lean from upright in degrees, and with `lean` (on by default) it leans
  toward where it is going, so the hairs trail behind the way a pulled brush's do.
- `roll` turns the handle about its own axis, which for a flat is the direction of its wide edge.
  By default a flat is held across its path.
- `facets` moves the hand in straight chords of that many canvas units instead of along the curve:
  at each corner the handle turns at once and the hairs whip round, beading a curve with a mark at
  every corner. A path drawn as a polyline does this at its own corners
  ([the sweep](paint_sweeps.md#the-hand) shows how it looks).

A gesture is a list of `TimedGesture.Sample(x, y, t, pressure, tilt, azimuth, roll)`, so you can
also build one yourself, from a pen's samples or a calculation. `faster(k)`, `pause(seconds)`,
`then(other)` and `reversed()` make new gestures from old ones.

Below, top left, a flick: pressed at the start and lifted off over a fast 400 mm/s stroke. Top
right, the same over a slow one. Second, a stroke that stops for 0.6 s halfway and carries on: the
brush held still on the canvas keeps laying paint, so the paint pools under it, and it lays thinner
paint afterwards. Third, a flat rolled through half a turn along its stroke, a ribbon that narrows
to the brush's edge and opens out again. Last, a filbert held upright and laid well over: upright,
only its tips touch, and it runs out sooner.

## A brush that keeps a set

Hair and hog bristle are keratin, which bends back elastically up to a strain of about 2% and
yields beyond it. A thick, stiff hog bristle reaches that strain at a smaller bend than a fine
sable hair, so ordinary painting leaves a brush nearly straight, but a hog pressed hard and
scrubbed sideways comes away splayed, and stays that way for its next strokes.
`brush.retainedBend` is the bend the hairs keep at rest, in radians averaged over every joint, 0
for a straight brush; a set comes slowly, over seconds of hard scrubbing, and goes again more
slowly still. `brush.set(...)` changes how the hairs behave:

- `friction`, static and kinetic, against the surface (0.35 and 0.25 by default);
- `yieldDegrees`, the bend past which a joint yields (from the fibre's thickness and the 2% strain
  by default);
- `plasticity`, how fast a yielded joint takes on its bend, per second, and `recovery`, how fast a
  set straightens again;
- `cohesion`, how strongly the liquid in a wet brush draws its hairs together: 1 draws a full
  brush's tips to a point, more pulls harder and closer, and below 0 pushes nearby hairs apart;
- `clumping`, which way it does it: 0 (the default) draws the tips of neighbouring hairs together,
  1 joins any wet hairs that come near each other by liquid bridges that snap when stretched, so the
  brush gathers into clumps; between, a blend; past 1 or below 0, more or the reverse;

  brush fans open) and `splayScatter` (each bundle of hairs buckling its own way).

`stroke(gesture, brush, ...)` can vary any of the last five along a stroke: give it a function of
the gesture's sample, such as `{ s -> 0.2 + 0.2 * PaintNoise.along(s) }`.

The defaults are estimates for hair and hog bristle. Any value that makes physical sense is
accepted: friction can't be negative.

## Keeping a brush

A moving brush keeps its paint or water, and the set of its hairs, from one stroke to the next. A
`PaintToolbox` keeps it by name with the other tools (`tools.dynamicBrush("hog")`), and
`brush.state()` and `DynamicBrush.restore(state, kind)` snapshot it exactly: every hair's
position and rest bend, and every bristle's paint. [AI4 paints](ai4_painting.md) keeps its
painter's moving brushes this way, so rewinding a conversation brings back a brush as splayed as
it was then.

## What is simulated

| | how | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The hairs | chains of segments under position-based dynamics (Verlet integration, constraint projection, 1 ms steps): each segment keeps its length, each joint is pulled toward its rest angle, more strongly the stiffer the hair | simulated |
| Contact | a node below the surface (paper, dry paint, wet paint) is put back on it | simulated |
| Friction | Coulomb's: a node sticks until its slip exceeds static friction times how hard it presses, then slides against kinetic friction | simulated |
| Splay | a hair pressed into the surface is pushed out from the brush's middle by `splay` (in `BrushConfig`) times how far it is pressed in, against the same grip: hard enough, a flat parts in two | an approximation of buckling by one number |
| A set | a joint bent past its yield (2% strain at the surface of a fibre whose thickness is estimated from the brush's stiffness) moves its rest angle toward the bend, and recovers slowly | simulated, with estimated rates |
| Clumping | by default the liquid in a full brush draws neighbouring tips together; with `clumping` 1, a liquid bridge forms where two wet hairs come near each other and pulls them together, harder toward the tips and the wetter and thinner the paint, and snaps when they are pulled a few spacings apart, further the more liquid it holds, so splay tears a wet brush into clumps | the tip pull is one strength; the bridges are simulated, their strength and reach estimates |
| Oil paint | each of the brush's dense bristles follows the hair nearest it and trades paint where it touches, through claude-paint's own paint model | the paint is claude-paint's; the contact is Field's |
| Watercolour | every touching hair trades with the sheet over a disc a clump of hairs wide, through the [watercolour](watercolor.md) model | simulated |
| Hair count | 16–64 hairs stand for the thousands in a real brush; the dense bristles copy their hair's contact; hairs do not collide with each other except through their bridges | approximated |

# Brushes with moving hairs

An ordinary [PaintCanvas](paint_canvas.md) brush places its bristles by rule: they follow the
path, and the tips trail a little behind. `canvas.dynamicBrush(...)` makes a brush whose hairs are
simulated instead. Each hair is a chain of short segments that bends, drags on the surface, sticks
and slides, splays when it is pressed and springs back when it is lifted. Where the hairs touch,
they lay and pick up paint, oil or watercolour. A brush pressed hard and dragged sideways for long
enough keeps a set, as a real one does.

Because the hairs have mass and stiffness, it matters how the hand moves, not only where. A
`TimedGesture` gives the brush's position over time, how hard it presses, and how the handle is
tilted and turned. The same path drawn slowly, fast, with a pause, tilted or rolled gives different
marks.

Here is a round brush drawn along the same curve at 20, 80 and 300 mm/s, and then right to left.
The slow stroke lays the most paint and runs out first; the fast one lays thinner paint and carries
it further.

with an ordinary brush.

## Gestures

`canvas.gesture(line, speed, pressure, tilt, lean, roll)` turns an FLine into a `TimedGesture`:

- `speed` is in mm/s along the path, so the time a stroke takes depends on the canvas's `sizeMm`.
- `pressure` is one value, a start and an end, or a profile at evenly spaced points along each
  subpath. At 0 the tips just touch, at 1 the ferrule is pressed down by 60% of the hairs' length,
  and more presses harder still. Below 0 the brush is lifted clear of the surface, so a stroke that
  ends below 0 leaves the paper.
- `tilt` is the handle's lean from upright in degrees, and with `lean` (on by default) it leans
  toward where it is going, so the hairs trail behind the way a pulled brush's do.
- `roll` turns the handle about its own axis, which for a flat is the direction of its wide edge.
  By default a flat is held across its path.
- `facets` moves the hand in straight chords of that many canvas units instead of along the curve:
  at each corner the handle turns at once and the hairs whip round, beading a curve with a mark at
  every corner. A path drawn as a polyline does this at its own corners
  ([the sweep](paint_sweeps.md#the-hand) shows how it looks).

A gesture is a list of `TimedGesture.Sample(x, y, t, pressure, tilt, azimuth, roll)`, so you can
also build one yourself, from a pen's samples or a calculation. `faster(k)`, `pause(seconds)`,
`then(other)` and `reversed()` make new gestures from old ones.

Below, top left, a flick: pressed at the start and lifted off over a fast 400 mm/s stroke. Top
right, the same over a slow one. Second, a stroke that stops for 0.6 s halfway and carries on: the
brush held still on the canvas keeps laying paint, so the paint pools under it, and it lays thinner
paint afterwards. Third, a flat rolled through half a turn along its stroke, a ribbon that narrows
to the brush's edge and opens out again. Last, a filbert held upright and laid well over: upright,
only its tips touch, and it runs out sooner.

## A brush that keeps a set

Hair and hog bristle are keratin, which bends back elastically up to a strain of about 2% and
yields beyond it. A thick, stiff hog bristle reaches that strain at a smaller bend than a fine
sable hair, so ordinary painting leaves a brush nearly straight, but a hog pressed hard and
scrubbed sideways comes away splayed, and stays that way for its next strokes.
`brush.retainedBend` is the bend the hairs keep at rest, in radians averaged over every joint, 0
for a straight brush; a set comes slowly, over seconds of hard scrubbing, and goes again more
slowly still. `brush.set(...)` changes how the hairs behave:

- `friction`, static and kinetic, against the surface (0.35 and 0.25 by default);
- `yieldDegrees`, the bend past which a joint yields (from the fibre's thickness and the 2% strain
  by default);
- `plasticity`, how fast a yielded joint takes on its bend, per second, and `recovery`, how fast a
  set straightens again;
- `cohesion`, how strongly the liquid in a wet brush draws its hairs together: 1 draws a full
  brush's tips to a point, more pulls harder and closer, and below 0 pushes nearby hairs apart;
- `clumping`, which way it does it: 0 (the default) draws the tips of neighbouring hairs together,
  1 joins any wet hairs that come near each other by liquid bridges that snap when stretched, so the
  brush gathers into clumps; between, a blend; past 1 or below 0, more or the reverse;
- `splay`, `splayFan` (0 every pressed hair pushed out alike, 1 the outer ones furthest, so the
  brush fans open) and `splayScatter` (each bundle of hairs buckling its own way).

`stroke(gesture, brush, ...)` can vary any of the last five along a stroke: give it a function of
the gesture's sample, such as `{ s -> 0.2 + 0.2 * PaintNoise.along(s) }`.

The defaults are estimates for hair and hog bristle. Any value that makes physical sense is
accepted: friction can't be negative.

the fresh brush lays a full band.

## Watercolour

`brush.loadWater(canvas, paint, fill)` loads a moving brush with
[watercolour](watercolor.md) instead, and from then on its hairs trade water and pigment with the
sheet wherever they touch it. How far the water on them reaches into the paper's tooth depends on
how hard the brush is pressed and how full it is, so a nearly dry brush, light and fast, catches
only the top of the tooth. Below, three strokes on rough paper with the brush full, a quarter full
and nearly dry:

## A finished piece

Broad black gestures in the manner of Robert Motherwell's *Elegies* and the Tachistes need a big
brush and a big canvas, real ones: here two metres of canvas and a house painter's brush about
15 cm wide, with soft, uneven hairs (`stiffness = 0.5`, `ragged = 0.5`), held together
(`splay = 0.0`) so each slab stays one band.
Fat black paint, stiff enough to hold its edge (`stiff = 0.5`, `oil = 1.5`), laid as a thin film
(`lay = 0.8`) from a half-loaded brush (`amount = 0.5`), so the brush tracks show through it. Each
movement is fast, 260 to 320 mm/s, and ends lifted off the canvas (pressure `-0.2`), which is where
the edges come from: the hairs drag dry and part as they leave. The ovals spiral out from their
middles, so their outer edge is painted last, as the brush runs out.

```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/paint_gestures/elegy.png" alt="a wide abstract painting in black on an off-white canvas: three tall vertical slabs of black alternating with two large black ovals squeezed between them, like an elegy. Each slab ends at the bottom in a fringe of dry, streaked bristle marks where the brush lifted off, and each oval's last turn trails away to the right in loose grey streaks of hair" wait="20" timeout="600" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20" requires="paint" name="elegy" embed=true}

val h = canvas.heightUnits

// a house painter's brush: soft, uneven hairs held together, laying a thin film of fat black
val housePainter = BrushConfig(stiffness = 0.5, ragged = 0.5, splay = 0.0, lay = 0.8, run = 1100.0)
fun brush(width: Double) = canvas.dynamicBrush(BrushKind.HogFlat, width, hairs = 48, segments = 6, config = housePainter)
    .load(rgb(0.05, 0.045, 0.04), hiding = 0.65, stiff = 0.5, oil = 1.5, amount = 0.5)

// an oval spiralling out from its middle, so its edge comes last, as the brush runs dry
fun oval(cx: Double, cy: Double, rx: Double, ry: Double): FLine {
    val line = FLine()
    line.breakNext()
    for (i in 0..120) {
        val u = i / 120.0
        val a = PI / 2 + 2 * PI * 1.8 * u
        val r = 0.2 + 0.8 * u
        line.lineTo(cx + rx * r * cos(a), cy + ry * r * sin(a))

    canvas.stroke(canvas.gesture(FLine().moveTo(x, 25).lineTo(x + 8, h - 25), speed = 260.0,
        pressure = [0.7, 1.0, 0.9, 0.4, -0.2], tilt = 25.0), brush(width))
// and two ovals between them
for ((cx, cy, rx) in [Triple(300.0, 250.0, 120.0), Triple(690.0, 230.0, 140.0)])
    canvas.stroke(canvas.gesture(oval(cx, cy, rx, 170.0), speed = 320.0,

## Keeping a brush

A moving brush keeps its paint or water, and the set of its hairs, from one stroke to the next. A
`PaintToolbox` keeps it by name with the other tools (`tools.dynamicBrush("hog")`), and
`brush.state()` and `DynamicBrush.restore(state, kind)` snapshot it exactly: every hair's
position and rest bend, and every bristle's paint. [AI4 paints](ai4_painting.md) keeps its
painter's moving brushes this way, so rewinding a conversation brings back a brush as splayed as
it was then.

## What is simulated

| | how | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The hairs | chains of segments under position-based dynamics (Verlet integration, constraint projection, 1 ms steps): each segment keeps its length, each joint is pulled toward its rest angle, more strongly the stiffer the hair | simulated |
| Contact | a node below the surface (paper, dry paint, wet paint) is put back on it | simulated |
| Friction | Coulomb's: a node sticks until its slip exceeds static friction times how hard it presses, then slides against kinetic friction | simulated |
| Splay | a hair pressed into the surface is pushed out from the brush's middle by `splay` (in `BrushConfig`) times how far it is pressed in, against the same grip: hard enough, a flat parts in two | an approximation of buckling by one number |
| A set | a joint bent past its yield (2% strain at the surface of a fibre whose thickness is estimated from the brush's stiffness) moves its rest angle toward the bend, and recovers slowly | simulated, with estimated rates |
| Clumping | by default the liquid in a full brush draws neighbouring tips together; with `clumping` 1, a liquid bridge forms where two wet hairs come near each other and pulls them together, harder toward the tips and the wetter and thinner the paint, and snaps when they are pulled a few spacings apart, further the more liquid it holds, so splay tears a wet brush into clumps | the tip pull is one strength; the bridges are simulated, their strength and reach estimates |
| Oil paint | each of the brush's dense bristles follows the hair nearest it and trades paint where it touches, through claude-paint's own paint model | the paint is claude-paint's; the contact is Field's |
| Watercolour | every touching hair trades with the sheet over a disc a clump of hairs wide, through the [watercolour](watercolor.md) model | simulated |
| Hair count | 16–64 hairs stand for the thousands in a real brush; the dense bristles copy their hair's contact; hairs do not collide with each other except through their bridges | approximated |

??? aside "Where the code is"
    The hairs are `native/field-paint/vendor/paint/src/field/bristles.rs`, Field's addition to
    alice's [claude-paint](https://github.com/aliceisjustplaying/claude-paint) crate; oil paint
    goes through claude-paint's own bristle `exchange`, which `VENDORED.md` lists among the places
    Field opened up in alice's code. `DynamicBrushTest` checks contact, tilt, the set,
    keeping and restoring, watercolour's books, and gesture headings.

See also: [Paint settings, swept](paint_sweeps.md), where one gesture is painted with each setting in
turn, [Paint and pencil from FLines](paint_canvas.md), [Watercolour and ink](watercolor.md),
