# Typography as geometry — a string becomes contours A string in Field is geometry. Field reads the font's own Bézier outlines, so a word can be extruded, marched, sampled, clustered or animated like any other shape. Every function used below is listed, with its documentation, in the [Graphics](reference/graphics.md) reference.
| what you want | where it is | |---|---| | a font at a size; a glyph's rings; a laid-out string with per-glyph handles | `typography.kt` — `Typeface`, `Glyph`, `GlyphContour`, `TextLayout`, `PlacedGlyph` | | text on a curve, word wrap, measuring | `typography.kt` — `TextLayout.onCurve`, `textCircle`, `wrapText`, `textWidth` | | letters → `FLine`, `TriMesh`, `ScalarField3D`, `Img`, point clouds | `typography_field.kt` | | a figure in a box output | `typography_field.kt` — `Box.showText`, `Box.showTextGrid`, `TextLayout.metricsFLines` |
## Hello, legibility Load a face, lay out a word, and fill its outlines into an image: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/typography_examples/word.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="640" padding="14"} :::static val face = typeface("SansSerif", 140.0) val word = layoutText("Handgloves", face) // rasterizeText is a scanline fill over the contours this family extracted. Not drawString. showImgGrid( "Handgloves — %d contours, %d of them counters, %.0f units wide" .format(word.contourCount, word.holeCount, word.advanceWidth) to rasterizeText(word, 1600, 380), columns = 1, cellSide = 900, ) ``` ![The word Handgloves in white sans-serif on black, every counter open](assets/typography_examples/word.png) `rasterizeText` fills the word's contours itself rather than asking the system to draw text, so the image is exactly the geometry the rest of this page works with. ## The winding convention, and the control arm A counter (the hole in `o`, `e`, `a`, `B`) is only a hole if something says so. Field's text contours follow one rule: > A ring's signed area is `½Σ(xᵢyᵢ₊₁ − xᵢ₊₁yᵢ)` in text space. **Outer contours are positive; holes > are negative.** Nesting depth, how many other rings of the same glyph contain this one, is > authoritative: even depth is an outer ring, odd depth is a hole. A ring whose area sign disagrees > with its depth is reversed on the way out. Skia and Java2D both fill **non-zero**, so a counter survives exactly because its ring runs the other way and cancels its bowl. Take the convention away and the letters fill in. Below: identical filler, identical fill rule, identical rings, with the hole rings reversed in the middle cell. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/typography_examples/winding.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1180" h="620" padding="14"} :::static :::fold one face, one window, so the three cells are strictly comparable val face = typeface("SansSerif", 220.0) val layout = layoutText("open", face) val window = layout.bounds :::endfold // The control arm is one argument. Same filler, same NON_ZERO rule, same rings — only their // direction differs, and NON_ZERO cancels a +1 outer against a −1 hole to leave a counter. val withConvention = rasterizeText( layout, 900, 460, window = window, fillRule = TextFillRule.NON_ZERO, rings = layout.toContours(honourHoles = true), ) val withoutConvention = rasterizeText( layout, 900, 460, window = window, fillRule = TextFillRule.NON_ZERO, rings = layout.toContours(honourHoles = false), ) // EVEN_ODD counts crossings and ignores direction, depending on nesting parity instead. Over // correct rings it must produce the IDENTICAL raster — two independent rules agreeing. val evenOdd = rasterizeText(layout, 900, 460, window = window, fillRule = TextFillRule.EVEN_ODD) :::fold measure the ink and the worst per-pixel disagreement, then draw the three cells var worst = 0.0 for (y in 0 until withConvention.height) for (x in 0 until withConvention.width) { worst = maxOf(worst, kotlin.math.abs(withConvention.at(x, y, 0) - evenOdd.at(x, y, 0)).toDouble()) } // Captions are drawn by montage's own 5x7 bitmap table and are clipped to the cell, so keep // them short enough to survive. showImgGrid( "convention on — %.1f%% ink".format(100 * withConvention.inkFraction()) to withConvention, "convention off — %.1f%% ink".format(100 * withoutConvention.inkFraction()) to withoutConvention, "EVEN_ODD: max diff %.5f".format(worst) to evenOdd, columns = 3, cellSide = 380, ) :::endfold ``` ![The word open three times: counters open, counters filled solid, and counters open again under the even-odd rule](assets/typography_examples/winding.png) The counters of `o` and `p` close up in the middle cell and the ink fraction rises to prove it. The `e` survives in **both**, because its aperture is open to the outside: it was never a closed ring, so there is nothing for a winding rule to get wrong. The third cell is the cross-check. `EVEN_ODD` ignores direction entirely, so over correct rings it must produce the *identical* raster, and the worst per-pixel difference printed in its caption is `0.00000`. Reverse the hole rings and the two rules diverge, which makes `EVEN_ODD` a quick check on rings you have built yourself. ## The rings themselves This box draws the outer rings and the hole rings of `aeg` separately, then together, then filled: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/typography_examples/rings.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1080" h="640" padding="14"} :::static val layout = layoutText("aeg", typeface("Serif", 240.0)) // Every ring of the layout, still classified: depth is containment, isHole is depth parity, // signedArea is the direction that classification forced. val rings = layout.toContours() :::fold one closed FLine per ring, tinted by classification val lines = rings.map { ring -> fline { ring.points.forEachIndexed { i, p -> if (i == 0) moveTo(p.x, p.y) else lineTo(p.x, p.y) } lineTo(ring.points[0].x, ring.points[0].y) color = if (ring.isHole) vec(1.0, 0.55, 0.28, 0.95) else vec(0.5, 0.82, 1.0, 0.95) thickness = 1.8 } to ring.isHole } val signs = rings.joinToString(" ") { if (it.signedArea > 0) "+" else "−" } showPlaneGrid( "outer rings — depth even, area positive (${rings.count { !it.isHole }})" to lines.filter { !it.second }.map { it.first }, "hole rings — depth odd, area negative (${rings.count { it.isHole }})" to lines.filter { it.second }.map { it.first }, "all ${rings.size} rings, signs $signs" to lines.map { it.first }, "the same layout, filled" to layout.toFLines(filled = true, stroked = false, thickness = 1.0), columns = 2, cellWidth = 460, cellHeight = 250, window = layout.bounds, ) :::endfold ``` ![Four panels of the letters a e g: three outer rings, four hole rings floating where the counters are, both together, and the filled result](assets/typography_examples/rings.png) Seven rings for `aeg`: three outer and four holes, because the double-storey `g` contributes two. In the hole panel those four little loops float in space exactly where the counters are. A letter is a ring *system*, and that panel is the system with its outer rings taken away. ## What layout decided `layoutText` takes AWT's advances and kerning pairs and adds the things AWT does not do: `\n`, letter-spacing, alignment, and a mutable transform handle per glyph. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/typography_examples/layout.png" wait="3.5" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="1160" padding="14"} :::static :::fold one face, and prose to wrap val face = typeface("SansSerif", 120.0) val prose = wrapText( "Type is geometry that happens to be legible, and legibility is the one test " + "a plausible looking picture cannot pass.", face.atSize(44.0), maxWidth = 620.0, ) :::endfold // Identity one: kerning off, no tracking — the line is the sum of its advances. Two different // AWT paths (accumulated pen positions vs per-glyph metrics) that have to agree. val plain = layoutText("minimum", face.withKerning(false)) val drift = plain.advanceWidth - plain.glyphs.sumOf { it.glyph.advance } // Identity two: tracking adds one gap per INTER-GLYPH space, not one per glyph. The trailing gap // nobody asked for is the classic off-by-one, and the advance boxes below show where it went. val t = 0.16 * face.size val tight = layoutText("TYPE", face) val loose = layoutText("TYPE", face, tracking = t) :::fold draw the metrics diagram, then the same wrapped paragraph in all three alignments // Two figures, so two CHANNELS: a second display on the same channel replaces the first. showPlaneGrid( "tracking 0 — %.0f units; advanceWidth − Σadvances = %.1e".format(tight.advanceWidth, drift) to (tight.metricsFLines() + tight.advanceBoxFLines() + tight.toFLines(thickness = 1.0)), "tracking 0.16em — %.0f units, i.e. exactly %d gaps × %.1f wider" .format(loose.advanceWidth, tight.glyphs.size - 1, t) to (loose.metricsFLines() + loose.advanceBoxFLines() + loose.toFLines(thickness = 1.0)), channel = "metrics", columns = 1, cellWidth = 880, cellHeight = 240, window = afield.app.protocol.Rect(-20.0, -face.ascent - 20, loose.advanceWidth + 40, face.lineHeight + 40), ) showImgGrid( *TextAlign.entries.map { a -> a.name.lowercase() to rasterizeText(layoutText(prose, face.atSize(44.0), align = a, lineSpacing = 1.12), 700, 380) }.toTypedArray(), channel = "alignment", columns = 3, cellSide = 290, ) :::endfold ``` ![Two baselines of TYPE with ascent and descent guides and one advance box per glyph, the second visibly looser, above the same four-line paragraph set left, centred and right](assets/typography_examples/layout.png) The first two panels diagram the *decisions* rather than the letters: `metricsFLines()` draws baseline, ascent and descent, and `advanceBoxFLines()` draws one box per glyph, including for a space, which has no glyph to draw and is why the boxes are useful. Compare the two rows and the extra space is visibly *between* the letters and not after the last one. Word wrap measures with the real layout, so it is correct for the tracking and kerning you are actually going to use, and all three alignments come off the same wrapped string. ## Text on a curve `onCurve` does not distort a glyph. It looks the glyph's advance-box centre up at that **distance** along the path, using `FLine.cursor()`'s arc-length table (the same machinery `sampleByDistance` and `byDashing` use), and then sets that glyph's `rotation` and `pivot`. So the letters stay letters, the spacing is even in distance rather than in curve parameter, and a multi-line layout follows the curve in bands instead of collapsing onto it. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/typography_examples/on_a_curve.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="940" h="1080" padding="14"} :::static :::fold a face, a string, and a cubic to bend the second one along val face = typeface("SansSerif", 78.0) val ring = layoutText("AROUND AND AROUND", face, tracking = 7.0) val wave = fline { moveTo(0.0, 0.0) cubicTo(300.0, -240.0, 720.0, 240.0, 1020.0, 0.0) } :::endfold // Size the circle to the text rather than the text to the circle: a circumference equal to the // layout's width means the string closes exactly, with no gap and no overlap at the seam. val circle = textCircle(radius = ring.advanceWidth / (2 * Math.PI)) val onCircle = ring.onCurve(circle, align = TextAlign.CENTER) val onWave = layoutText("a rolling line of type", face, tracking = 2.0).onCurve(wave, align = TextAlign.CENTER) :::fold the filled rasters, then the paths they sit on // Two figures, two CHANNELS: a second display on one channel replaces the first. showImgGrid( "circumference %.1f vs width %.1f".format(circle.arcLength(), ring.advanceWidth) to rasterizeText(onCircle, 620, 620), "%d of %d glyphs turned".format(onWave.glyphs.count { kotlin.math.abs(it.rotation) > 0.05 }, onWave.glyphs.size) to rasterizeText(onWave, 620, 620), channel = "rasters", columns = 2, cellSide = 420, ) showPlaneGrid( "the circle it sits on — original untouched: ${ring.glyphs.all { it.isUntransformed }}" to ([circle.copy { color = vec(0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 0.6); thickness = 1.0 }] + onCircle.toFLines(thickness = 1.0)), "the cubic it sits on" to ([wave.copy { color = vec(0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 0.6); thickness = 1.0 }] + onWave.toFLines(thickness = 1.0)), channel = "paths", columns = 2, cellWidth = 430, cellHeight = 430, ) :::endfold ``` ![AROUND AND AROUND set clockwise around a circle beside a rolling line of type following an S-curve, and below them the circle and the cubic drawn as thin paths with the same letters as outlines sitting on them](assets/typography_examples/on_a_curve.png) The first caption gives **998.7** of circumference against **998.9** of layout width. Two tenths of a unit over a thousand is what "closes exactly" costs, and it is the reason to size the circle from the text rather than the other way round. The lower row is the paths themselves with the letters as outlines on them, and its caption records that `onCurve` returned a **copy**, so the straight layout is still straight and can be bent along something else. ## Kinetic typography Every `PlacedGlyph` carries `offset`, `rotation`, `scale` and `pivot`, and the pivot defaults to the glyph's own visual centre, so a bare `rotation = 0.3` spins each letter about itself and looks like what you meant. One layout, computed once, and a function of elapsed seconds written into it. (`animate { }` and the `AnimationClock` it reads are Field's frame model; if you want to know what a frame actually is, and what stops one, see [Frames and the animation loop](animation_time_model.md).) ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin video="assets/typography_examples/kinetic.mp4" capture="box" open-outputs="true" wait-output="true" wait-output-kind="display" execution="launch" duration="8" fps="20" timeout="300" w="900" embed=true name="typography-kinetic" alt="the word KINETIC with a travelling wave of rotation, scale and vertical lift running left to right through the letters, each letter turning about its own centre inside a frame that never moves"} :::static :::fold the face, the layout, and a window fixed from the widest the wave will ever get val face = typeface("SansSerif", 150.0) val layout = layoutText("KINETIC", face, tracking = 16.0) // A FIXED frame, not fit-to-contents: left to rescale to each frame's own bounds the letters would // move and the picture would stand still. # Typography as geometry — a string becomes contours A string in Field is geometry. Field reads the font's own Bézier outlines, so a word can be extruded, marched, sampled, clustered or animated like any other shape. Every function used below is listed, with its documentation, in the [Graphics](reference/graphics.md) reference.
| what you want | where it is | |---|---| | a font at a size; a glyph's rings; a laid-out string with per-glyph handles | `typography.kt` — `Typeface`, `Glyph`, `GlyphContour`, `TextLayout`, `PlacedGlyph` | | text on a curve, word wrap, measuring | `typography.kt` — `TextLayout.onCurve`, `textCircle`, `wrapText`, `textWidth` | | letters → `FLine`, `TriMesh`, `ScalarField3D`, `Img`, point clouds | `typography_field.kt` | | a figure in a box output | `typography_field.kt` — `Box.showText`, `Box.showTextGrid`, `TextLayout.metricsFLines` |
## Hello, legibility Load a face, lay out a word, and fill its outlines into an image: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/typography_examples/word.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1000" h="640" padding="14"} :::static val face = typeface("SansSerif", 140.0) val word = layoutText("Handgloves", face) // rasterizeText is a scanline fill over the contours this family extracted. Not drawString. showImgGrid( "Handgloves — %d contours, %d of them counters, %.0f units wide" .format(word.contourCount, word.holeCount, word.advanceWidth) to rasterizeText(word, 1600, 380), columns = 1, cellSide = 900, ) ``` ![The word Handgloves in white sans-serif on black, every counter open](assets/typography_examples/word.png) `rasterizeText` fills the word's contours itself rather than asking the system to draw text, so the image is exactly the geometry the rest of this page works with. ## The winding convention, and the control arm A counter (the hole in `o`, `e`, `a`, `B`) is only a hole if something says so. Field's text contours follow one rule: > A ring's signed area is `½Σ(xᵢyᵢ₊₁ − xᵢ₊₁yᵢ)` in text space. **Outer contours are positive; holes > are negative.** Nesting depth, how many other rings of the same glyph contain this one, is > authoritative: even depth is an outer ring, odd depth is a hole. A ring whose area sign disagrees > with its depth is reversed on the way out. Skia and Java2D both fill **non-zero**, so a counter survives exactly because its ring runs the other way and cancels its bowl. Take the convention away and the letters fill in. Below: identical filler, identical fill rule, identical rings, with the hole rings reversed in the middle cell. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/typography_examples/winding.png" wait="3.0" capture="box" open-outputs="true" w="1180" h="620" padding="14"} :::static :::fold one face, one window, so the three cells are strictly comparable val face = typeface("SansSerif", 220.0) val layout = layoutText("open", face) val window = layout.bounds :::endfold // The control arm is one argument. Over // correct rings it must produce the IDENTICAL raster — two independent rules agreeing. val evenOdd = rasterizeText(layout, 900, 460, window = window, fillRule = TextFillRule.EVEN_ODD) :::fold measure the ink and the worst per-pixel disagreement, then draw the three cells var worst = 0.0 for (y in 0 until withConvention.height) for (x in 0 until withConvention.width) { worst = maxOf(worst, kotlin.math.abs(withConvention.at(x, y, 0) - evenOdd.at(x, y, 0)).toDouble()) } // Captions are drawn by montage's own 5x7 bitmap table and are clipped to the cell, so keep // them short enough to survive. showImgGrid( "convention on — %.1f%% ink".format(100 * withConvention.inkFraction()) to withConvention, "convention off — %.1f%% ink".format(100 * withoutConvention.inkFraction()) to withoutConvention, "EVEN_ODD: max diff %.5f".format(worst) to evenOdd, columns = 3, cellSide = 380, ) :::endfold ``` ![The word open three times: counters open, counters filled solid, and counters open again under the even-odd rule](assets/typography_examples/winding.png) The counters of `o` and `p` close up in the middle cell and the ink fraction rises to prove it. The `e` survives in **both**, because its aperture is open to the outside: it was never a closed ring, so there is nothing for a winding rule to get wrong. The third cell is the cross-check. `EVEN_ODD` ignores direction entirely, so over correct rings it must produce the *identical* raster, and the worst per-pixel difference printed in its caption is `0.00000`. The hole count comes from ring nesting in the plane; the genus comes // from counting the mesh's vertices, edges and faces. They have no reason to agree unless the // extruder is right. val holesIn2D = layoutText("o", face).holeCount // A 2D area against a 3D volume: a shoelace sum times the depth, against the divergence theorem // over the triangles. A dropped cap triangle or a wall wound the wrong way breaks it. val expected = layoutText("o", face).glyphs.sumOf { it.glyph.inkArea } * 46.0 val measured = layoutText("o", face).toMesh(depth = 46.0, yUp = false).volume() :::fold draw them — note what is NOT here: flatShaded() // flatShaded() un-welds every triangle, and the genus in these labels is topology() over whatever // you hand it — so a flat-shaded copy would label itself "genus null, watertight false" while // looking identical. Unnecessary as well: both renderers // apply shadedNormals to a mesh that arrives without normals for you. showMeshGrid( "o — genus ${o.genus()}, 2D hole count $holesIn2D, watertight ${o.isWatertight()}" to o, "l — genus ${l.genus()}, watertight ${l.isWatertight()}" to l, channel = "letters", columns = 2, cellWidth = 420, view = MeshView(yawDegrees = 26.0, pitchDegrees = 16.0, distance = 3.2), ) showMesh( word, channel = "word", view = MeshView(yawDegrees = 22.0, pitchDegrees = 14.0, distance = 2.6, width = 820, height = 340), title = "extruded from the same contours the raster filled", caption = "'o': ink area × depth = %.0f, mesh volume %.0f, relative difference %.2e" .format(expected, measured, kotlin.math.abs(expected - measured) / expected), ) :::endfold ``` ![An extruded lowercase o as a ring you can see through beside an extruded l as a solid slab, and the word mesh extruded in 3D](assets/typography_examples/mesh.png) **Genus 1 for `o` and 0 for `l`**: a 2D count — rings nested at odd depth — agreeing with a 3D one, χ over the mesh's vertices, edges and faces. The extruded volume agrees with the ink area times the depth in the same way. Either identity breaks on a dropped cap triangle, a wall wound the wrong way or an unpunched counter, so they are a quick check on any mesh you build from text. and the four surfaces val grid = sdf.distanceField // showImgGrid rather than showImg: showImg sends its caption as a separate output message, // which the image then replaces, so the caption never survives to the page. montage only ever // scales a tile DOWN, so upscale the grid first or it lands as a 340px thumbnail. showImgGrid( "signed distance field, %dx%d grid, deepest %.0f".format(grid.nx, grid.ny, grid.deepestInside()) to grid.toImg().upscaleNearest(2), channel = "grid", columns = 1, cellSide = 880, ) showMeshGrid( "marchingCubes on the letters — The sign convention is `mesh_sdf.kt`'s, **negative inside**, the opposite of `GlyphContour.signedArea`'s: an area's sign says which way a ring runs, a distance's sign says which side of the ink you are on. ## Letters as point clouds The plainest bridge is even-by-arc-length samples along the outlines. From here `vec2KMedoids` finds the strokes, `vec2DelaunayGraph` triangulates a word, and the agents in [Spatial Artificial Life](alife_examples.md) will happily eat a headline. ## Loading a font The examples above use the logical families `SansSerif` and `Serif`, which every machine has. To ask for a particular font, or load one from a file: ```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin} typeface("SansSerif", 64.0) // logical family: always resolves Typefaces.named("Futura", 64.0, strict = true) // throws instead of substituting silently Typefaces.firstAvailable("Futura", "Avenir", size = 64) // the first one this machine actually has Typefaces.fromFile("/path/to/Whatever.ttf", 64.0) // Font.createFont, not registered globally ``` `Typefaces.available()` lists the installed families. `SansSerif` and `Serif` map to different real fonts on different machines, so the pictures above will look a little different on yours. The ring counts, genus and winding do not change. ## Run it yourself The page's boxes are also the [`typography_worked_example`](agent_transcripts.md#typography_worked_example) starting point, a document you can open and edit.

before: # Watercolour and ink A [PaintCanvas](paint_canvas.md) made with `PaintCanvas.paper(...)` is a sheet of watercolour paper, and water laid on it moves by itself. It flows downhill and into the hollows of the paper, sinks in, wicks along the fibres and evaporates. The pigment it carries settles, stains or dries in place. A wash dries with a darker edge and the paper's grain in it, clean water dropped into a damp wash pushes its colour out into a backrun, and a nearly dry brush skips over rough paper. No rule paints these effects in; they come from what the water and the pigment do. The oil paint, brushes and canvas underneath are alice's [claude-paint](https://github.com/aliceisjustplaying/claude-paint) (see [Paint and pencil from FLines](paint_canvas.md)). The water model is Field's own addition to it, written on the same pixel grid, so pencil and oil paint work over a watercolour and feel the paper's tooth. It needs the same native library (`./gradlew buildPaintNative`). Here is a sheet of cold-pressed paper, a round watercolour brush and a sky, with hills painted once the sky had dried: ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/watercolor/first.png" alt="a small watercolour study on off-white cold-pressed paper. The top is a sky of four overlapping horizontal brushstrokes of blue that have run together into one band, deeper above and paler below, with a fine grain where a little more pigment gathered in the hollows of the paper's texture. Below, two broad wavy strokes of warm grey-brown for the hills, with the same fine grain and crisp edges and a little white paper left between them" wait="20" timeout="600" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20" requires="paint" name="first" embed=true} :::static import afield.graphics.paint.* val sheet = PaintCanvas.paper(700, aspect = 1.5, paper = Paper.ColdPress, sizeMm = 200.0, seed = 3) val brush = sheet.waterBrush(width = 70.0) // the sky, in overlapping strokes while it is wet brush.load(Watercolors.ultramarine * 3.0 + Watercolors.burntSienna * 0.5) sheet.wash(FLine().moveTo(60, 90).lineTo(940, 90).moveTo(940, 135).lineTo(60, 135), brush, speed = 50.0) brush.load(Watercolors.ultramarine * 1.2, fill = 0.8) sheet.wash(FLine().moveTo(60, 180).lineTo(940, 180).moveTo(940, 225).lineTo(60, 225), brush, speed = 50.0) // let it dry, then the hills over it sheet.dry() brush.load(Watercolors.burntSienna * 3.0 + Watercolors.ultramarine * 2.0) val hills = FLine().moveTo(40, 420).cubicTo(250, 300, 450, 420, 960, 340) sheet.wash(hills, brush, pressure = [1.0], speed = 30.0) sheet.wash(FLine().moveTo(40, 470).lineTo(960, 450), brush, pressure = [1.0], speed = 30.0) sheet.dry() display("main", sheet.png()) ``` What is new compared with oil: - **Paint is pigment in water.** `Watercolors.ultramarine * 3.0` is ultramarine at 3 µg of pigment per mm³ of water (1 is pale, 6 strong), and `+` mixes pigments. The brush holds water, not paint: `load(paint, fill)` fills its belly to `fill` of what it holds. - **Time passes.** Every stroke takes as long as it would at its `speed` (mm/s), and the water moves for that long. `waitSeconds(s)` lets more time pass and `dry()` waits until the sheet is dry. A stroke laid into a wet one runs into it; a stroke over a dry one keeps its edge. - **The sheet has a real size.** `sizeMm` is how wide the paper is, so a brush 70 units wide on a 200 mm sheet is 14 mm across. Water and pigment are counted in mm³ and µg, and the paper's texture is in mm, so the same strokes on a smaller sheet look coarser. ## Papers `Paper` has five sheets. Each is a physical make-up, how much water it holds, how fast it drinks and wicks, its grain, tooth and sizing, so the same drop behaves differently on each because the water does. Below, one 15 µl drop of sumi ink on each, left to dry: cold press, hot press, rough, xuan (rice paper) and blotting paper. On the sized cotton sheets the drop stands as a small dome and dries where it stood, a crisp black dot; xuan drinks it at once and feathers it out along its long fibres; blotting paper takes it in quickly and softens its edge. ```diffstatic_runner {data-lang=kotlin screenshot="assets/watercolor/papers.png" alt="five squares of paper side by side, each with one dried drop of black ink in the middle. On cold press, hot press and rough paper the drop is a small, crisp, round black dot, a little ragged on the rough sheet. On xuan paper the ink has spread into a much larger, soft grey disc that feathers out into the paper in fine radial streaks. On blotting paper it is a round black dot a little larger than the first three, with a soft edge" wait="20" timeout="600" capture="box" open-outputs="true" padding="20" requires="paint" name="papers" embed=true} :::static import afield.graphics.paint.* val sheets = Paper.entries.map { paper -> PaintCanvas.paper(220, aspect = 1.0, paper = paper, sizeMm = 50.0, seed = 2).also { sheet -> sheet.drop(500.0, 500.0, Watercolors.sumi * 3.0, volumeMm3 = 15.0) sheet.dry() } } display("main", pngRow(sheets)) ``` `sheet.paper` reports the make-up: how much water the sheet holds saturated (`capacityMicrons`), how fast dry paper takes up standing water (`absorbMicronsPerSecond`), how fast water wicks through it (`wickMm2PerSecond`), its tooth (`roughnessMicrons`) and how deep water must be to advance onto dry paper (`pinMicrons`). On wetter paper the paint flies further and leaves more of its colour at that edge. Pressing harder widens the stroke and pushes the hairs into the paper's hollows. How full the brush is decides how far the water on it reaches down into the tooth: a full brush floods across everything; a nearly dry one, light and fast, touches only the top of the tooth, which is drybrush. Drybrush wants paint nearly as strong as it comes off the pan, 20 to 80 µg/mm³, since so little water reaches the paper. Its `pigments` are one `PigmentLedger` each, in µg, with the pigment in each state: - `suspended` in the water on the paper, moving with it; - `carried` in the water in the paper's pores, moving with it; - `deposited`, settled out but loose: water flowing through carries it on; - `glued`, dried in place in its gum: rewetting lifts it slowly, a brush faster; - `bound`, stained into the fibres: it no longer lifts; - and `added`, `taken`, `runoff` and `sealed` (under oil paint), what came and went. What is on the sheet always equals what was added less what left, to rounding, and `imbalanceMm3` and `imbalance` say by how much. Coordinates are the same as any canvas: 1000 units wide, y down. - `evaporation(micronsPerSecond)` sets how fast open water evaporates: about 0.15 µm/s in still air at 20 °C and 50 % humidity, several times that in a warm draught. - `marangoni(newtonsPerMetre)` sets how far paint lowers the surface tension of the water it is in (0.008 by default): it drives the spreading of wet-in-wet. 0 turns it off. - `dispersion(mm2PerSecond)`, 0 by default, adds an extra spreading of pigment through standing water. It is not simulated (see below), a dial for when you want softer mixing. - `saveState(path)`, `PaintCanvas.load(path)` and `copy()` keep the water and every pigment in it exactly, wet or dry, and the copy carries on as the original would have. ## How the water model works The water model keeps, for every pixel, the water standing on the sheet and the water in its pores, and for each pigment its mass in each of the five states of the books above. On every step: | | how | simulated or approximated | | --- | --- | --- | | Flow on the surface | a thin film driven by gravity and the paper's relief (lubrication theory), the sheet's tilt included | simulated; surface tension is not, so shapes finer than about 3 mm (water's capillary length) are not resolved | | Wetting dry paper | water advances only from a film deeper than the paper's `pinMicrons` | an approximation of contact-angle hysteresis by one number | | Absorption and wicking | surface water drawn into the pores at the paper's sizing rate; capillary diffusion through the sheet, faster along the fibres | simulated, with a linear stand-in for the slowing of uptake as the sheet fills | | Evaporation | from the surface water, faster near the edge of a wet patch (Deegan et al., *Nature* 389, 1997); then from the pores | simulated; the dark edge of a dried wash is the flow toward the edge carrying pigment, not a rule | | Settling | each pigment falls through the water at its Stokes velocity, from its density and particle size | simulated | | Diffusion to the fibres | fine particles diffuse through the water to the paper (Stokes–Einstein) and stick there, the same amount per area wherever the water stands deep enough | simulated | | Texture in a wash | a wash's surface lies level, so it stands deeper over the paper's hollows and leaves more there; how much shows depends on the paper's relief | simulated; the reliefs are estimates | | Granulation | coarse pigment gathering in the hollows beyond what the water's depth leaves there, so that ultramarine speckles more than phthalo | not simulated: here every pigment follows the depth about equally | | Filtering and staining | particles larger than the pores stay on the surface; staining pigments adsorb onto the fibres | simulated with estimated rates | | Backruns | settled pigment is carried on by water flowing through it; drying glues it down | simulated | | Blooms | paint lowers surface tension, and the cleaner water pulls the surface outward (Marangoni flow) | simulated with an estimated tension drop; the wetting agents are carried and adsorbed | | Colour | Kubelka–Munk absorption and scattering per pigment, laid over the sheet | simulated optics; wet paper's darkening is a fixed factor | | The paper | flocs of fibre and the felt's texture | generated, not made by a simulated papermaking | | Every number for a paper or pigment | | an estimate in the reported range, not a measurement of a product | Time steps are adaptive: short while water is moving fast, long while the sheet is only drying. The wetter and larger the sheet, the longer a wait takes to compute; a 700-pixel sheet drying a full wash takes some seconds. ??? aside "Where the code is" The model is in `native/field-paint/vendor/paint/src/field/aqueous.rs` (the sheet, its water and pigments) and `watercolor.rs` (brushes, drops and washes). It lives inside the vendored claude-paint crate so that it can share the canvas's grid, height and optics, but it is Field's code, not alice's; `VENDORED.md` there lists exactly what Field changed in alice's files. `WaterMediaTest` checks the books, saving and restoring, the brushes and gestures.
